stem: A periodontal probe reads 5 mm from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket. What is this measurement called?
ex: PD runs from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket. CAL adds recession to PD; GR runs from the CEJ to the gingival margin.
why: Probing depth is measured from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket, exactly what this reading describes.
CAL is measured from the CEJ, not the gingival margin: it is probing depth plus recession.
Recession runs from the CEJ to the gingival margin; it says nothing about how deep the pocket is.
Radiographic bone loss is read on a film, not measured with a probe in the pocket.

cue: CAL = PD + GR, and a hidden CEJ makes GR negative: 7 + (-4) = 3.
stem: Probing depth is 7 mm, and the CEJ is felt 4 mm apical to the gingival margin (no visible recession). What is the clinical attachment level?
ex: CAL = PD + GR using signed GR. Here GR = -4 (CEJ is subgingival), so CAL = 7 + (-4) = 3 mm of attachment loss.
why: With the CEJ 4 mm below the margin, GR is -4, so CAL = 7 + (-4) = 3 mm.
7 mm is the probing depth; it ignores the 4 mm of pocket that sits above the CEJ on enamel.
11 mm adds the 4 mm instead of subtracting it; a subgingival CEJ makes GR negative.
4 mm is the CEJ-to-margin distance (the negative recession), not the attachment loss.

likely.t: Stage from CAL and bone loss, never from probing depth alone

stem: Tooth X: 2 mm probing depth with 4 mm of visible recession (CAL 6 mm). Tooth Y: 7 mm probing depth, CEJ felt 4 mm subgingival (CAL 3 mm). Which tooth is more maintainable for the patient, despite its higher attachment loss?
ex: Recession makes CAL look worse on paper, but a shallow, accessible 2 mm pocket is far easier for a patient to brush and floss than a deep 7 mm pocket.
why: A shallow 2 mm pocket is easy for the patient to brush and floss, so it is more maintainable even with more CAL on paper.
A 7 mm pocket is too deep for home care to reach, so it is harder to maintain despite its lower CAL.
The two differ: maintainability depends on pocket depth the patient can clean, not on CAL alone.
Both can be maintained; the question is which is easier, and the shallow pocket wins.

likely.t: Stage from CAL and bone loss, never from probing depth alone

stem: Which radiograph is preferred over a horizontal bitewing when screening for periodontal bone loss, and why?
choices: Vertical bitewing — less likely to miss bone loss on one arch
Panoramic — gives the most site-specific detail
Occlusal film — best shows interproximal bone
ex: A horizontal bitewing can fail to capture bone loss on one of the two arches; vertical bitewings extend the field and are preferred when bone loss is a concern.
why: Vertical bitewings extend the field, so bone loss on either arch is less likely to be cut off the film.
A panoramic gives an overview but the least site-specific detail of these films.
Occlusal films show the arch from above and are not used to read interproximal crestal bone.
The horizontal bitewing is the one being replaced here: it can miss bone loss on one of the two arches.

stem: Name the two findings that must both be present for a bleeding 5 mm probing depth to represent periodontitis rather than gingivitis.
answer: Attachment loss AND radiographic bone loss at that site. A deep probing depth alone can occur in plaque-induced gingivitis (which can reach 4–5 mm) without any attachment or bone loss — so probing depth by itself never proves periodontitis.

likely.t: Stage from CAL and bone loss, never from probing depth alone

stem: A tooth has 1 mm of mesial and 1 mm of distal recession (some interproximal attachment loss present), but 6 mm of buccal recession — clearly more than either interproximal measurement. What recession type is this?
ex: Interproximal attachment loss is present, ruling out RT1. Buccal loss (6 mm) exceeds interproximal loss (1 mm), which is the definition of RT2.
why: Interproximal loss is present and buccal loss exceeds it (6 mm vs 1 mm): that is RT2.
RT1 means no interproximal attachment loss, and this tooth has some.
RT3 needs interproximal loss greater than buccal loss; here buccal loss is far greater.
The measurements given are enough: interproximal loss present and smaller than buccal loss defines RT2.

likely.t: Recession types from the chart: RT1, RT2, RT3 and root coverage

stem: Which recession type is not treated with a root-coverage attempt, because it will not succeed?
choices: All types are treated the same way
ex: In RT3, interproximal attachment loss exceeds buccal loss — coverage cannot be achieved and is not attempted.
why: In RT3, interproximal attachment loss exceeds buccal loss, so root coverage cannot be achieved and is not attempted.
RT1 (no interproximal loss) is the type where full root coverage is most predictable.
RT2 can still be treated with root coverage, though full coverage is less predictable than RT1.
The types are distinguished precisely because they predict different root-coverage outcomes.

likely.t: Recession types from the chart: RT1, RT2, RT3 and root coverage

stem: Match each recession type to its definition.
ex: Jepsen, Caton et al., 2018 World Workshop, Workgroup 3.

stem: Under the 2018 World Workshop classification, what replaced the older separate categories of 'chronic periodontitis' and 'aggressive periodontitis'?
choices: A single "Periodontitis" category, staged and graded
Nothing — the old terms are still used clinically
ex: Both old terms were merged into one Periodontitis category; individualized severity/behavior is now captured through staging and grading instead.
why: Chronic and aggressive periodontitis were merged into one Periodontitis category, described by stage and grade.
There are no 'slow' and 'fast' categories; speed of progression is captured by the grade.
The old terms were retired in the 2017/2018 classification; staging and grading replaced them.
Necrotizing periodontitis is its own separate category, not a merger of chronic and aggressive.

stem: What bleeding-on-probing threshold is used before a case is called gingivitis, to account for inter-examiner probing variability?
ex: Two or three bleeding spots on a full-mouth chart are not, by themselves, enough to diagnose gingivitis.
why: Gingivitis needs bleeding at 10% or more of sites, so a few stray bleeding spots don't make the diagnosis.
Any bleeding at all would over-diagnose; two or three spots can come from probing variability.
50% is far above the cutoff; gingivitis is diagnosed from 10% of sites.
25% is not the threshold; the gingivitis cutoff is 10% of sites bleeding.

stem: A patient on a calcium channel blocker has gingival overgrowth. Does the medication cause this by itself?
answer: No. Drug-associated gingival overgrowth (calcium channel blockers, cyclosporine) only develops in the presence of existing plaque and poor oral hygiene — the medication alone does not cause it.

stem: A treated periodontitis patient is stable on 3-month maintenance with no bleeding and shallow probing depths, though radiographs show old bone loss. What is the correct diagnosis today?
ex: A stable, well-maintained patient is not re-staged — they are described as healthy on a reduced periodontium.
why: A stable, well-maintained treated patient with no bleeding and shallow pockets has health on a reduced periodontium.
Without bleeding and with shallow pockets the disease is not active; old bone loss alone does not make it active Stage 3.
The periodontium is not intact: there is old bone loss, so it is a reduced periodontium.
Necrotizing disease is painful with necrotic papillae, nothing like this stable patient.

likely.t: Maintenance works: the Becker tooth-loss figures

stem: Which statement about reversibility is correct?
choices: Gingivitis can return fully to health; periodontitis cannot fully return to its original attachment level
Both gingivitis and periodontitis are fully reversible
Periodontitis is reversible, gingivitis is not
ex: There is a point of no return between the two: gingivitis resolves completely with plaque control, while periodontitis leaves permanent attachment loss even after successful treatment.
why: Gingivitis resolves fully with plaque control; periodontitis leaves permanent attachment loss even after treatment.
Periodontitis is not fully reversible: lost attachment does not simply return with treatment.
Gingivitis is reversible; only periodontitis has passed the point of no return.
This flips them: gingivitis is the reversible one, periodontitis is not.

stem: What distinguishes necrotizing periodontal disease from typical gingivitis or periodontitis?
choices: It is very painful and brings patients in for urgent care
It is usually found on routine probing, since it rarely causes symptoms
It is diagnosed mainly from radiographic bone loss
It is seen mostly in healthy patients with good immune function
ex: Ordinary periodontitis and gingivitis are not painful; necrotizing disease is, with decapitated papillae and a grayish pseudomembrane. Severely compromised patients include those with HIV/AIDS and CD4 <200.
why: Necrotizing disease is very painful, with decapitated papillae and a grayish pseudomembrane, so patients come in urgently.
That describes ordinary gingivitis and periodontitis, which are painless and found on probing.
It is a clinical diagnosis (pain, necrotic papillae, pseudomembrane), not a radiographic one.
It is associated with compromised patients, such as HIV/AIDS with CD4 under 200, not healthy ones.

stem: A patient has a vertical bone defect measuring 4 mm. What does this make the case automatically, regardless of the CAL numbers?
ex: Vertical bone loss ≥3 mm is one of three automatic Stage 3/4 triggers, alongside Class II–III furcation involvement and tooth loss due to periodontitis.
why: A vertical bone defect of 3 mm or more is an automatic Stage 3/4 trigger, so 4 mm makes it at least Stage 3.
Stage 1 is mild disease; a 3 mm+ vertical defect rules it out.
Grade describes rate of progression, not the defect depth; vertical defects affect the stage.
Necrotizing periodontitis is a separate painful condition, not defined by a vertical defect.

likely.t: Stage from CAL and bone loss, never from probing depth alone

stem: What grade should a clinician assume by default, before looking for evidence to shift it up or down?
ex: Clinicians should initially assume Grade B (moderate progression) and seek specific evidence to move to A or C.
why: Grade B (moderate progression) is the default; you then look for evidence to move to A or C.
Grade A needs evidence of slow progression; it is not the starting assumption.
Grade C needs evidence of rapid progression or risk factors; it is not the default.
There is a default: assume Grade B until evidence shifts it.

likely.t: Grading: start at B; the bone-loss/age ratio, smoking and HbA1c

stem: A 30-year-old patient has 50% bone loss on their worst tooth. What does that bone-loss/age ratio suggest on its own?
ex: 50% ÷ 30 years ≈ 1.7, well above the 1.0 cutoff that points toward rapid progression, Grade C.
why: 50% bone loss at age 30 gives a ratio of about 1.7, above 1.0, which points to Grade C.
A ratio under 0.25 suggests Grade A, but this case's ratio is about 1.7.
The ratio here is about 1.7, not 1, and Grade B covers the 0.25-1.0 range.
The bone loss and age are enough to compute the ratio: 50/30 ≈ 1.7.

cue: Bone loss outpacing age (ratio over 1) = Grade C on its own, no smoking or diabetes needed.
stem: Case A (30-year-old, systemically healthy) has isolated bone loss into the middle third of the root at #30 with a 7 mm probing depth, and no smoking or diabetes. What is her diagnosis?
ex: Middle-third bone loss and a 7 mm pocket put her in Stage 3; her bone-loss/age ratio exceeds 1, which is Grade C even without smoking or diabetes as modifiers.
why: Middle-third bone loss with a 7 mm pocket is Stage 3, isolated means localized, and a ratio over 1 is Grade C.
Her disease is isolated (localized), not generalized, and nothing points to Stage 4 or to Grade B.
Middle-third bone loss and a 7 mm pocket are periodontitis, not gingivitis.
Stage 1 is mild coronal loss; middle-third bone loss and a 7 mm pocket are Stage 3, and her ratio is Grade C.

stem: Case B, a 41-year-old, has bone loss confined to #2 and #15, with a bone-loss/age ratio that is borderline Grade B on its own. A finding in his history pushes his grade up to C. Which finding would do that?
choices: Smoking 10 or more cigarettes a day
Smoking fewer than 10 cigarettes a day
ex: Case B is a heavy smoker. Smoking 10 or more cigarettes a day is a grade modifier that pushes the case to Grade C outright, regardless of the bone-loss/age calculation. Fewer than 10 a day or an HbA1c under 7% point to Grade B, and furcation involvement changes the stage, not the grade.
why: Smoking 10 or more cigarettes a day is a grade modifier that pushes the case straight to Grade C.
Fewer than 10 cigarettes a day points to Grade B, not C.
Diabetes only modifies grade at HbA1c of 7% or more; below 7% points to Grade B.
Furcation involvement changes the stage (Class II-III is a Stage 3 trigger), not the grade.

stem: Case E has an HbA1c of 6.1%. Why does her periodontitis stay Grade B instead of moving to Grade C?
choices: Her HbA1c is below the 7% threshold that would push a case to Grade C
Grade C only applies to smokers
Her age protects her from Grade C
ex: The diabetes grade modifier only applies at HbA1c ≥7%. At 6.1%, her control is good enough that diabetes is not acting as a modifier.
why: The diabetes modifier only applies at HbA1c of 7% or more; at 6.1% it doesn't push her to Grade C.
Diabetes does affect grading: an HbA1c of 7% or more pushes a case to Grade C.
Grade C is also reached through diabetes (HbA1c ≥7%) or a high bone-loss/age ratio, not just smoking.
Age only enters grading through the bone-loss/age ratio; it doesn't protect anyone from Grade C.

likely.t: Grading: start at B; the bone-loss/age ratio, smoking and HbA1c

cue: "Screen, Stage, Grade, Plan": a quick look, then fine-tune the stage, then the grade, then treat.
stem: Put the 4-step approach to diagnosing periodontitis in order.
steps: Initial screening of full-mouth radiographs, probing depths, and missing teeth
Fine-tune the stage using maximum CAL/RBL and case complexity
Determine the grade from progression evidence and modifiers
Build the treatment plan from the stage and grade
ex: Kornman & Papapanou's 4-step practical approach, 2018.

stem: At flap reflection, bone remains on the buccal wall, the lingual wall, and against the neighboring tooth — only the involved root surface itself lacks bone. How many walls does this defect have, and what does that mean for regeneration?
choices: 3 walls — the best prognosis for regeneration
ex: The more walls remaining around a defect, the better the case for regrowing bone, PDL, and cementum.
why: Buccal, lingual and proximal walls remain: a 3-wall defect, which has the best prognosis for regeneration.
A 1-wall defect has only one wall left; this one has three, which is the best case.
A crater is a 2-wall defect with both proximal walls lost; here three walls remain.
A 4-wall defect would surround the root on every side; here the root surface itself lacks bone, leaving three walls.

cue: Crater = a dip between two teeth: both proximal walls gone, buccal and lingual left standing.
stem: Bone is lost on both proximal root surfaces of a defect, leaving only the buccal and lingual walls. What is this specific 2-wall pattern called?
ex: When both neighboring teeth have lost bone at the same site, the resulting 2-wall defect is called a crater.
why: A 2-wall defect with bone lost on both proximal sides, leaving buccal and lingual walls, is a crater.
A trench is not one of the defect types taught; the 2-wall interdental pattern is a crater.
A furcation is bone loss between the roots of a multirooted tooth, not between neighboring teeth.
A dehiscence is missing bone over the facial or lingual root surface, not an interdental crater.

stem: Why are the coronal/middle/apical thirds of the root measured from where bone should be in health, rather than from the CEJ itself?
answer: In health, bone already sits about 1.5–2 mm apical to the CEJ. Starting the thirds at the CEJ would overestimate how much destruction has actually occurred.

Definitive crown first, then periodontal therapy

stem: Where does caries control fit in the treatment sequence?
choices: It is part of Phase I therapy, alongside SRP
It only happens after all surgical therapy is finished
It is unrelated to periodontal treatment planning
It always follows delivery of the final RPD

why: Caries control is bundled into Phase I with SRP, since open lesions are hard to instrument and to keep clean.
Caries is not deferred to after surgery; cavitated surfaces hold plaque and undermine Phase I.

The final RPD comes late in the plan; caries control happens early, in Phase I.

stem: At which appointment is the final decision about surgical (Phase II) therapy actually made?
choices: The first scaling and root planing visit

stem: How does periodontal maintenance differ from a routine prophylaxis?
answer: Maintenance is for patients who have had periodontal disease and treatment and need closer recall — often every 3 months — to catch recurrence early and reinforce risk-factor control. Prophylaxis is for patients without periodontitis risk, typically on a 6-month recall. They are not the same visit.

likely.t: Maintenance works: the Becker tooth-loss figures

choices: Patients who were treated but did not return for maintenance
ex: Treated-without-maintenance patients lost about 0.22 teeth/year versus 0.11 teeth/year for treated-with-maintenance patients — roughly double.
why: Treated patients who skipped maintenance lost about 0.22 teeth per year, double the 0.11 of maintained patients.
Untreated patients are a separate comparison; the 'double' figure is treated-without-maintenance vs maintained.
Antibiotic use was not the comparison group in the Becker data.
Gingivitis-only patients were not the group compared; the data compared periodontitis patients by maintenance.

likely.t: Maintenance works: the Becker tooth-loss figures

stem: Under which CDT code does periodontal charting/screening fall, as part of a new-patient exam?
choices: D4341 — Periodontal Scaling and Root Planing

stem: Two patients both have interdental CAL ≥5 mm, bone loss into the middle third of the root, and 7 mm pockets. What moves one of them from Stage 3 to Stage 4?
choices: ≥5 teeth lost to periodontitis, or a need for complex rehabilitation
A vertical bone defect of 3 mm or more on at least one tooth
A bone-loss/age ratio above 1.0 at the worst tooth
Smoking 10 or more cigarettes a day
ex: Stages 3 and 4 share the same CAL (≥5 mm) and bone-loss (middle third or beyond) cutoffs. They are separated by tooth loss to periodontitis (≤4 teeth = Stage 3, ≥5 = Stage 4) and by whether the case needs complex, multidisciplinary rehabilitation (masticatory dysfunction, mobility ≥2, bite collapse, fewer than 20 teeth left). A ≥3 mm vertical defect is a Stage 3 finding; the bone-loss/age ratio and smoking set the grade, not the stage.
why: Stage 4 is set by losing 5 or more teeth to periodontitis or needing complex rehabilitation.
A 3 mm+ vertical defect is a Stage 3 finding; it doesn't separate Stage 3 from Stage 4.
The bone-loss/age ratio sets the grade, not the stage.
Smoking is a grade modifier, so it can't move a case from Stage 3 to Stage 4.

likely.t: Stage from CAL and bone loss, never from probing depth alone

stem: In the 2017 classification, what does grading describe that staging does not?
choices: The rate of progression and how the patient is likely to respond
The current severity and extent of attachment loss
How complex the case will be to manage
Whether the disease is localized or generalized
ex: Staging captures severity at presentation (CAL, bone loss, teeth lost) plus the complexity of management. Grading estimates how fast the disease is moving and how the patient will respond, which is where risk (smoking, HbA1c) enters the diagnosis. Localized vs. generalized is the extent, written in front of the stage.
why: Grading estimates how fast the disease is moving and how the patient will respond, where risk factors enter.
Severity and extent of attachment loss at presentation are what staging captures.
Complexity of management is part of staging, not grading.
Localized vs generalized is the extent, written in front of the stage, not what the grade describes.

stem: Which suture material is natural, monofilament, resorbs fastest (7–10 days), but handles very poorly?

stem: What does a reverse cutting needle do differently from a standard cutting needle?
choices: Its flat side faces the tissue on the upward pass, reducing tearing
It only cuts on the downward pass
It has no cutting edge at all
It is used only with non-resorbable sutures

why: Its cutting edge sits on the outer curve, so the flat side faces the wound edge on the way up and is less likely to tear through.

stem: A larger needle-curvature arc produces what kind of bite?
ex: The more of a circle the needle's arc covers, the deeper it drives into the tissue for the same entry point, so a larger curvature gives a deeper bite.
why: The more of a circle the arc covers, the deeper the needle drives for the same entry point.
A shallower bite comes from a flatter, smaller arc.
Curvature does change bite depth: a larger arc goes deeper.

stem: In suture sizing, what does a larger number mean, and what does that require?

why: Sizes run backwards: a bigger number is a thinner strand, and thinner material needs more throws to hold.
A larger number means a smaller diameter, not a larger one.
A larger number is a thinner strand; it does need more knots, but it isn't thicker.

stem: Which technique is essential for larger bone-augmentation procedures and prevents flap-margin inversion, but can constrict blood supply and cause necrosis if overtightened?
ex: The horizontal mattress is the augmentation workhorse: it everts the margins and resists tension over a graft. Pulled too tight, it strangles the blood supply to the incision edge, which can lead to necrosis and dehiscence.

Continuous locking is for long edentulous spans and alveoloplasties; its risk is the whole line unraveling.

ex: The vertical mattress gives maximal approximation and eversion without pressing down on the papilla, which is why it is used for papillae in the esthetic zone and to close oro-antral communications.

stem: Which technique risks the entire suture line coming undone if a single throw fails, especially with monofilament or high-glide material?
ex: Used for edentulous long-span areas, alveoloplasties, and apicoectomies — the bites sit close together for a good seal, but the whole line depends on every throw holding.

stem: Which flap design offers limited access and is difficult to advance because of lateral attachment, making it best for minor augmentation or simple implant placement?
ex: A sulcular flap has no vertical release, so the tissue stays attached on both sides. That limits access and makes it hard to advance, which is fine for minor augmentation or a simple implant.
why: A sulcular flap has no vertical release, so it stays attached laterally: limited access, hard to advance.
A trapezoidal flap has two vertical releases, giving wide access and easy coronal advancement.
Split thickness describes how deep the flap is reflected, not its outline or access.
Papilla-sparing describes how papillae are handled, used for esthetic and regenerative surgery.

likely.t: A flap's base must be wider than its free edge

stem: A flap that leaves periosteum on the bone and reflects only the mucosa and submucosa is called what?
ex: Split thickness means the periosteum stays on the bone and only mucosa and submucosa are lifted. A full-thickness (mucoperiosteal) flap takes the periosteum with it and exposes bone.
why: A split-thickness flap leaves periosteum on the bone and lifts only mucosa and submucosa.
A full-thickness (mucoperiosteal) flap takes the periosteum with it and exposes bone.
Sulcular describes the incision outline (no vertical release), not the depth of reflection.
Pyramidal describes the outline (one vertical release), not how deep the flap is reflected.

likely.t: Full vs partial thickness by procedure

stem: Flap designs are classified along three axes. Which of these is NOT one of them?
choices: Suture material used to close the flap
Placement of the flap after surgery relative to the CEJ
ex: Flaps are classified by bone exposure (full vs split thickness), by where the flap is placed afterwards relative to the CEJ (apical, coronal, not displaced), and by how the papillae are handled. Suture material is chosen separately.
why: Suture material is chosen separately; it is not one of the three ways flaps are classified.
Bone exposure (full vs split thickness) is one of the three classification axes.
Placement relative to the CEJ (apical, coronal, not displaced) is one of the three axes.
Papilla management (papilla-sparing or not) is one of the three axes.

likely.t: A flap's base must be wider than its free edge

stem: List the 5 surgical principles for incisions and flap design given in this lecture.
answer: 1) Firm, continuous incision stroke. 2) Incision at a distance from the lesion/bony defect. 3) Vertical incisions at the line angle of the tooth. 4) Periosteum reflected as an integral part of the flap. 5) The flap base as wide as its free edge.

likely.t: Vertical incisions at the line angle, never through the papilla

stem: Why must the base of a flap be at least as wide as its free edge?
choices: To protect the flap's blood supply
ex: A flap's blood vessels enter from its base. If the base is narrower than the free edge, the far end is starved of blood and can necrose.
why: Blood vessels enter from the base, so a narrow base starves the free edge and it can necrose.
Base width is about blood supply, not about making the flap easier to suture.
A wide base often means longer incisions; the reason is perfusion, not shorter cuts.
Base width has nothing to do with the periosteum; that is the full vs split thickness choice.

likely.t: A flap's base must be wider than its free edge

stem: A surgeon performs the exact same sulcus-following incision around tooth #8, which is present, and along an edentulous ridge where tooth #9 used to be. What are these two incisions called?
choices: Intrasulcular at #8, crestal at #9 — same technique, named by tooth presence
Crestal at #8, intrasulcular at #9 — named by where the scalpel blade enters
Both are called vertical incisions, since each runs along the long axis
Both are called pouch incisions, since neither releases the flap laterally
ex: Intrasulcular and crestal are the same physical incision. The name changes based only on whether a tooth is present at that site, not on any difference in technique.
why: Same incision: intrasulcular where a tooth is present (#8), crestal along the edentulous ridge (#9).
This reverses them: crestal is the edentulous-ridge name and intrasulcular the name around a tooth.
Vertical incisions are releasing cuts running apically, not ones that follow the sulcus or crest.
Pouch describes a flap design; the incisions themselves are named intrasulcular and crestal.

stem: Why would a surgeon drop a vertical incision instead of just extending the intrasulcular incision to more teeth?
choices: To gain more apical exposure without including teeth that don't need to be involved
Because vertical incisions heal faster than intrasulcular ones
Vertical incisions are required by law to be used before any bone graft
To avoid ever having to place a suture
ex: A vertical release opens the flap apically, so you reach bone and defects without dragging extra, uninvolved teeth into the surgery.
why: A vertical release opens the flap apically, reaching bone without dragging uninvolved teeth into surgery.
Vertical incisions don't heal faster; they're added for access.
There is no rule requiring vertical incisions before a bone graft.
Flaps with vertical releases still need sutures to close.

likely.t: Vertical incisions at the line angle, never through the papilla

stem: A root-coverage case needs a soft-tissue graft placed without disturbing the papillae at all. Which flap design fits?
ex: The envelope/pouch flap elevates only the buccal tissue and never reflects the papillae — exactly what a root-coverage graft needs.
why: The envelope (pouch) flap elevates only buccal tissue and never reflects the papillae.
A trapezoidal flap uses two vertical releases and reflects tissue widely, disturbing the area.
A soft-tissue graft needs a split-thickness bed for blood supply, and exposing bone doesn't spare papillae.
Extending a sulcular flap across 4 teeth reflects the papillae along the way.

cue: Trapezoid = two releases, a door on each side, so the flap slides up with no tension.
stem: A major vertical ridge-augmentation graft needs the flap to advance coronally with zero tension over the graft. Which flap design is built for that?
ex: Two releasing incisions, one on each side of the defect, let the flap stretch coronally without tension — a single vertical often can't reach that far without tearing.
why: Two releasing incisions let the trapezoidal flap advance coronally with tension-free closure over a big graft.
A sulcular flap has no release and is hard to advance, fine only for minor augmentation.
A pyramidal flap has only one release, often not enough reach for a major vertical graft.
An envelope flap has no vertical release and doesn't advance far.

stem: An implant needs onlay bone grafting around it, and the surgeon wants more access than a sulcular flap gives without opening both sides of the site. What's the fit?
ex: A pyramidal flap uses one vertical plus an intrasulcular incision across three teeth. It gives more exposure than a sulcular flap without the second release a trapezoidal flap needs, which is reserved for major augmentation. An envelope flap has no vertical release at all, and bone grafting needs a full-thickness flap, not a split-thickness one.
why: A pyramidal flap's single vertical release gives more access than a sulcular flap without opening both sides.
A trapezoidal flap opens both sides with two releases, reserved for major augmentation.
An envelope flap has no vertical release, so it gives even less access than needed here.
Bone grafting needs bone exposed, which means a full-thickness flap, not split thickness.

stem: Match each suture material family to an example the lecture named.
ex: Gut is the natural absorbable; Vicryl (polyglactin) and Monocryl (poliglecaprone) are synthetic absorbables; silk, ePTFE, Prolene (polypropylene) and nylon stay until removed.

cue: Sub-marginal = "cut it off": the incision sits below the margin and the strip of pocket wall is thrown away.
stem: A site probes 6 mm and needs its pocket surgically eliminated rather than the pocket wall reflected and repositioned. Which incision is designed for exactly this?
ex: Placed below the free gingival margin and excisional by design — a strip of pocket wall is cut away and discarded, not reflected back, leaving a shallower sulcus.
why: A sub-marginal incision sits below the gingival margin and cuts away a strip of pocket wall to eliminate the pocket.
An intrasulcular incision keeps the pocket wall and reflects it, rather than removing it.
A crestal incision is the same cut on an edentulous ridge; it doesn't remove pocket wall.
A vertical incision only releases the flap for access; it doesn't remove pocket tissue.

likely.t: The sub-marginal incision

stem: Why does a sub-marginal incision create recession, and is that a problem?
choices: It's created on purpose to eliminate a pocket — acceptable when pocket depth, not recession, is the problem being treated
It's always a complication that should be avoided
It only happens if the surgeon makes an error
It happens but resolves completely within a week
ex: A sub-marginal incision deliberately removes pocket wall. The recession that results is the point of the procedure when the problem being treated is pocket depth.
why: Removing pocket wall on purpose leaves recession, which is acceptable when pocket depth is the problem.
It isn't a complication: the recession is the intended result of eliminating the pocket.
It isn't an error; recession is built into how a sub-marginal incision works.
The tissue is excised, so the recession it creates doesn't resolve on its own.

likely.t: The sub-marginal incision

stem: An implant is being placed with simultaneous bone grafting. What flap thickness should be reflected, and why?
choices: Full thickness — the goal is to expose and graft bone
Split thickness — the goal is to protect the periosteum
Full thickness — split flaps can't be sutured closed
Split thickness — implants never need bone exposed
ex: Grafting bone around an implant needs the bone exposed, so the periosteum comes up with the flap: full thickness.
why: Grafting bone needs the bone exposed, so the periosteum is lifted with the flap: full thickness.
Split thickness leaves periosteum on the bone, which is the bed for soft-tissue grafts, not bone grafts.
Full thickness is right, but not because split flaps can't be sutured; they can be.
Implants with grafting do need bone exposed, so split thickness doesn't fit.

likely.t: Full vs partial thickness by procedure

stem: A soft-tissue graft is being placed to thicken keratinized tissue around a tooth. What flap thickness is reflected at the recipient site, and why?
choices: Split thickness — periosteum is left behind as a vascularized bed for the graft
Full thickness — more bone exposure helps grafts attach
Split thickness — because soft-tissue cases never bleed
Full thickness — periosteum would reject the graft
ex: A soft-tissue graft needs a blood supply from underneath, so the recipient site is split thickness: the periosteum left on the bone becomes the vascular bed the graft lives on.
why: The periosteum left on the bone is the vascular bed the soft-tissue graft lives on, so the site is split thickness.
Bone exposure doesn't help a soft-tissue graft attach; it needs a vascular periosteal bed.
Split thickness is right, but soft-tissue sites do bleed; the reason is the vascularized bed.
Periosteum doesn't reject grafts; it is what feeds them.

likely.t: Full vs partial thickness by procedure

stem: Harvesting a palatal connective tissue graft, which donor site is preferred and why?
choices: The molar area — more lamina propria, less fatty adipose tissue that would shrink after transplant
The premolar area — thinner tissue is easier to suture
The molar area — it has no risk of bleeding
The premolar area — it has more adipose tissue for bulk
ex: The premolar region carries proportionally more fatty adipose tissue beneath the epithelium; adipose tissue resorbs quickly once transplanted, so a graft that includes too much of it will visibly shrink.
why: The molar region has more lamina propria and less fatty tissue, which would shrink after transplant.
Premolar palatal tissue carries more adipose, which resorbs and shrinks the graft.
The molar area is preferred for tissue quality, but it still bleeds; the greater palatine vessels run there.
Adipose isn't wanted bulk: it resorbs after transplant, which is why the premolar area is avoided.

stem: Of the palate's three tissue layers (epithelium, connective tissue/lamina propria, adipose), which does a connective tissue graft keep?
ex: A CTG takes only the lamina propria. The epithelium is left on the palate (an FGG keeps it), and the fatty submucosa is trimmed off because it does not help the graft take.
why: A connective tissue graft keeps only the lamina propria; epithelium stays on the palate and fat is trimmed.
Keeping all three layers would include epithelium and fat, which a CTG leaves behind.
Epithelium plus connective tissue is a free gingival graft (FGG), not a CTG.
Adipose is trimmed off because it shrinks and doesn't help the graft take.

stem: Why is a braided suture generally avoided in favor of a monofilament, even though silk (braided) is still used for some cases?
answer: A braided suture's woven strands wick and trap bacteria the way a smooth monofilament strand doesn't, raising inflammation/infection risk. Silk is the accepted exception — its handling and ability to apically position tissue make it useful for osseous surgery and crown lengthening despite the tradeoff, and it's removed early (about 7 days).
ex: If a braided suture must be removed, wipe it with chlorhexidine gauze first so plaque trapped in the weave doesn't get dragged into the flap on the way out.

stem: A single interrupted suture in the esthetic zone risks pushing the papilla down and creating a black triangle. Which technique avoids this by approximating the flap edges rather than cinching down on top of the tissue?
ex: A single interrupted suture cinches down on top of the papilla. The vertical mattress pulls the flap edges together instead, so the papilla keeps its height and no black triangle forms.
why: The vertical mattress draws the flap edges together without pressing on the papilla, so it keeps its height.
Continuous locking is for long edentulous spans and alveoloplasties, not papilla preservation.
A sling repositions a flap around one tooth; the esthetic papilla technique taught is the vertical mattress.
Periosteal anchorage holds a flap to periosteum for apical or lateral repositioning.

stem: A patient with thin buccal tissue on the lower incisors is about to start orthodontic treatment that will push those teeth further buccally. What's the recommended sequence?
choices: Graft to thicken the tissue prophylactically before orthodontic movement begins
Start orthodontics and graft only if recession actually develops
Delay orthodontics indefinitely — thin tissue is a permanent contraindication
Graft after orthodontics is finished, regardless of what happens during treatment
ex: This is periodontal-orthodontic clearance: grafting ahead of the movement prevents the recession that pushing a tooth through thin tissue tends to cause, rather than treating it after the fact.
why: Thickening the tissue before moving the teeth prevents recession that pushing them through thin tissue tends to cause.
Waiting for recession means treating damage that grafting first would have prevented.
Thin tissue isn't a permanent contraindication; grafting first allows orthodontics to proceed.
Grafting after orthodontics misses the window; the recession risk is during the movement.

stem: Which risk-assessment system is applied to individual teeth and can be either diagnostic or therapeutic?
ex: McGuire & Nunn is the per-tooth system, and the only one that can be used both diagnostically (before treatment) and therapeutically. Kwok & Caton is whole-mouth; Miller & McEntire is molars only.
why: McGuire & Nunn is the per-tooth system and the only one usable both diagnostically and therapeutically.
Kwok & Caton is whole-dentition and therapeutic only.
Miller & McEntire covers molars only and is therapeutic only.
One of the systems does fit: McGuire & Nunn.

likely.t: Diagnostic vs therapeutic: only McGuire & Nunn works diagnostically

stem: Which system assesses the likelihood of achieving periodontal stability for the whole dentition, and is therapeutic only?
ex: Kwok & Caton scores the whole dentition on how likely the patient is to reach periodontal stability, and it is used therapeutically only.
why: Kwok & Caton scores the whole dentition on the likelihood of periodontal stability, therapeutically only.
McGuire & Nunn rates individual teeth on maintainability and can also be diagnostic.
Miller & McEntire rates molars only, on the likelihood of keeping them.
Hamp is a furcation classification (horizontal mm), not a prognosis system.

likely.t: Kwok & Caton (stability, whole dentition) and Miller & McEntire (molars)

stem: Which prognosis system applies only to molars?
ex: Miller & McEntire was built and studied on molars only, and it is quantitative, scoring factors like smoking and A1c.
why: Miller & McEntire was built and studied on molars only.
McGuire & Nunn applies to any tooth, rated one by one.
Kwok & Caton applies to the whole dentition.
Glickman is a furcation classification, not a prognosis system.

likely.t: Kwok & Caton (stability, whole dentition) and Miller & McEntire (molars)

cue: McGuire & Nunn = "Maintain" (M for M). Miller & McEntire = Molars retained. Kwok & Caton = Can it be stabilized?
stem: What does the McGuire & Nunn system assess?
choices: How easy the tooth is to maintain in the mouth
A numeric score of how likely a molar is to be retained
ex: McGuire & Nunn asks whether a tooth can be maintained (kept in the mouth) and how much effort that will take (good: easy to maintain; poor: kept only with significant effort). A numeric score of how likely a molar is to be retained is Miller & McEntire: molars only, quantitative. "Likelihood of stability" is Kwok & Caton, and the rate of progression is what grading describes.
why: McGuire & Nunn asks how easy the tooth will be to maintain.
That is Miller & McEntire: molars only, scored as a number. McGuire & Nunn rates any tooth by how easy it will be to keep.
Likelihood of periodontal stability is what Kwok & Caton assesses.
Rate of progression is what grading describes, not a prognosis system.

likely.t: McGuire & Nunn rates retention (maintainability); about 80% / 50% accurate

stem: Match each risk-assessment system to its scope.
ex: Scope is the quickest way to tell them apart: McGuire & Nunn rates single teeth, Kwok & Caton the whole mouth, Miller & McEntire molars only.

likely.t: Kwok & Caton (stability, whole dentition) and Miller & McEntire (molars)

stem: Which system(s) are strictly therapeutic — meaning they cannot be used purely diagnostically?
choices: All three systems are diagnostic only
None of the three are therapeutic
ex: Kwok & Caton and Miller & McEntire are therapeutic only. McGuire & Nunn is the one system that works either way.
why: Kwok & Caton and Miller & McEntire are therapeutic only; McGuire & Nunn works either way.
McGuire & Nunn isn't strictly therapeutic; it can also be used diagnostically.
None is diagnostic only; all three can be used therapeutically.
All three can be used therapeutically; two of them only therapeutically.

likely.t: Diagnostic vs therapeutic: only McGuire & Nunn works diagnostically

stem: How is McGuire & Nunn different from the other two risk-assessment systems in terms of when it can be used?
answer: McGuire & Nunn can be applied either before treatment planning (diagnostic) or to gauge response after treatment (therapeutic). Kwok & Caton and Miller & McEntire are described as therapeutic only.

likely.t: Diagnostic vs therapeutic: only McGuire & Nunn works diagnostically

cue: Kwok & Caton looks at the Whole mouth only; McGuire & Nunn can rate each tooth (or the whole mouth); Miller & McEntire only molars.
stem: Which of the three prognosis systems is given for the whole dentition, not tooth by tooth?
ex: Kwok & Caton is the whole-dentition system: it asks whether periodontal stability can be reached with treatment. McGuire & Nunn can be given for the whole dentition too, but it is also given tooth by tooth, and Miller & McEntire scores single molars.
why: Kwok & Caton judges the whole dentition: can periodontal stability be reached with treatment?

Miller & McEntire scores single molars.
Only Kwok & Caton works at the whole-dentition level alone; McGuire & Nunn is also given per tooth, and Miller & McEntire per molar.

likely.t: Kwok & Caton (stability, whole dentition) and Miller & McEntire (molars)

stem: What does P4 stand for in "P4 medicine", as the lecture defines it?
ex: Applied specifically to periodontal care, the lecture extends this to P5: personalized, preventive, predictive, participatory, periodontal.

stem: D1110 (prophylaxis) makes up 95.4% of cleaning codes in patients aged 50 to 64. What makes this figure notable?

It exactly matches expected periodontitis prevalence in that age group
It is lower than the share seen in patients 19-34
D1110 is not billed in patients over 50

cue: PISA: a ~34 mm² scratch in health vs a ~2,300 mm² open wound in perio, 60-70 times bigger.
stem: Roughly how much larger is the periodontal inflamed surface area (PISA) in a patient with mild-to-moderate periodontitis compared to a periodontally healthy patient?
choices: Roughly 60-70x larger (about 2,309 mm² vs. about 34 mm²)
About twice as large (roughly 70 mm² versus 34 mm² in a periodontally healthy patient)
About 10x larger (roughly 340 mm², about the size of a single deep pocket around one molar)

Healthy sulcus lining isn't inflamed; PISA measures inflamed surface, which grows enormously in disease.

stem: What does PISA stand for and what does it estimate?
answer: Periodontal Inflamed Surface Area — the total area of pocket epithelium facing active inflammation, used to illustrate how large an inflammatory burden periodontitis represents systemically.

stem: In the COPD trial discussed in lecture, how did actual subgingival (SRP) therapy compare to supragingival-only scaling?
choices: SRP produced roughly double the reduction in COPD exacerbation frequency
Both groups improved by the same amount
Neither group showed any respiratory benefit

why: Subgingival SRP cut COPD exacerbations about twice as much as supragingival scaling alone.
The groups differed: SRP gave roughly double the reduction.

stem: In the 12-month diabetes trial comparing intensive periodontal therapy to supragingival-only control therapy, what happened to HbA1c in each group?
choices: Neither group showed any HbA1c change

cue: Summed 0-4 scores = UniFe ("Unified" into one number); PRA is the hexagon picture.
stem: Which whole-patient risk tool scores smoking (cig/day), diabetic status (HbA1c), number of pockets ≥5mm, BOP%, and bone-loss/age ratio, each 0-4, into a single summed score?
ex: UniFe sums five 0–4 scores (cigarettes/day, HbA1c, pockets ≥5 mm, BOP %, bone loss/age) into one number. PRA is a hexagon diagram, not a summed score.
why: UniFe sums five 0-4 scores (cigarettes/day, HbA1c, pockets ≥5 mm, BOP%, bone loss/age) into one number.
PRA (Lang & Tonetti) is a hexagon spider-web diagram, not a single summed score.

stem: Per the risk-stratified maintenance protocol, how often should a low-risk patient get professional biofilm/calculus removal?
ex: In the risk-stratified protocol, low-risk patients get biofilm/calculus removal every 6 months. Moderate risk is every 4–6 months and high risk every 2–4 months.
why: Low-risk patients get biofilm and calculus removal every 6 months.
Every 3 months is too frequent for low risk; high risk is every 2-4 months.
Every 2-4 months is the high-risk interval.
Every 4-6 months is the moderate-risk interval.

likely.t: Risk-stratified maintenance intervals

stem: Per the risk-stratified maintenance protocol, how often should a high-risk patient get an oral exam/periodontal screening (separate from the comprehensive exam)?
choices: Screening is not scheduled separately for high-risk patients
ex: High-risk patients get a separate screening every 3 months on top of the 6–12-month comprehensive exam. Moderate risk is every 6 months, and low risk has no separate screening.
why: High-risk patients get a separate screening every 3 months, on top of the comprehensive exam.
Every 6 months is the moderate-risk screening interval.
Every 12 months is the outer limit of the comprehensive exam, not the high-risk screening.

likely.t: Risk-stratified maintenance intervals

stem: Why is a periodontally-treated maintenance patient with every site reading 3mm not automatically a candidate for a plain prophylaxis?
choices: Their long junctional epithelial attachment is inherently more prone to breaking down under inflammation than a healthy connective-tissue attachment
A 3mm reading is never accurate after periodontal treatment
Insurance will not reimburse a prophylaxis after periodontal treatment
Periodontal patients cannot reach 3mm probing depths
ex: After treatment the pocket is lined by a long junctional epithelium, not a new connective-tissue attachment. It breaks down more easily under inflammation, so a treated patient stays on periodontal maintenance even when every site reads 3 mm.
why: Treated pockets heal with a long junctional epithelium, which breaks down more easily than connective-tissue attachment.
A 3 mm reading can be accurate after treatment; the issue is the type of attachment underneath.
The reason is biological (long junctional epithelium), not insurance.

stem: Roughly how much more likely is a treated-but-non-maintained periodontitis patient to lose teeth compared to a treated-and-well-maintained patient?
choices: Tooth loss risk is unrelated to maintenance compliance
ex: Treated periodontitis patients who skip maintenance lose about twice as many teeth as those who keep their recall, so the treatment only holds if maintenance continues.
why: Treated patients who skip maintenance lose about twice as many teeth as those who keep recall.
They are not equally likely; skipping maintenance roughly doubles tooth loss.
Five times overstates it; the figure taught is about double.
Tooth loss clearly depends on maintenance: skipping it roughly doubles the rate.

stem: Why does periodontal maintenance land on roughly a 3-month interval for most patients?
answer: Pathogenic subgingival species begin re-establishing 4-8 weeks after treatment, and by about 9-11 weeks the subgingival microbiome can repopulate close to pre-treatment levels — a 3-month recall sits inside that recolonization window.

likely.t: Risk-stratified maintenance intervals

stem: Why are patients undergoing active orthodontic tooth movement typically seen for periodontal maintenance every 4-6 weeks rather than every 3 months?
choices: Inflammation during active tooth movement can uncouple bone formation from resorption, risking real bone loss if biofilm is not controlled tightly
Orthodontic brackets make 3-month scheduling physically impossible
Tooth movement eliminates the need for periodontal maintenance entirely
It matches a fixed insurance billing cycle
ex: During active tooth movement, inflammation can tip remodeling toward resorption and cause real bone loss, so biofilm is controlled more tightly, every 4–6 weeks.
why: Inflammation during tooth movement can tip remodeling toward resorption, so biofilm is controlled every 4-6 weeks.
Brackets don't make 3-month visits impossible; the shorter interval is about bone risk.
Tooth movement increases, not removes, the need for maintenance.
The interval comes from biology (bone remodeling), not insurance cycles.

stem: What is the number one reason patients decline a periodontal treatment plan, per the lecture's patient-trust data?
choices: Lack of trust in their dental provider
ex: 62% of patients delay treatment, switch providers, seek a second opinion, or refuse care because they disagree with or distrust the diagnosis.

Time is not the top reason in the lecture's data; trust is.

stem: On average, how much did patients report they would pay per tooth to avoid losing it, and what does that figure argue about cost as a barrier to care?
answer: About $633.63 per tooth. Patients are often willing to pay meaningfully to save a tooth, so cost is usually not the real barrier to accepting treatment; cost becomes an objection mainly when patients feel rushed, cannot ask questions, sense disagreement within the dental team, or are not offered options for managing the cost.

stem: Match each risk tier to its oral exam / periodontal screening interval.
pairs: Covered by the 6-12 month comprehensive exam, not scheduled separately
ex: Risk sets the screening interval: low risk relies on the 6–12-month comprehensive exam, moderate risk adds a screening every 6 months, and high risk every 3 months.

likely.t: Risk-stratified maintenance intervals

stem: In the McGuire & Nunn system, what actually decides which prognosis category a tooth lands in?
choices: How well the tooth can be maintained (kept in the mouth)
How likely the tooth is to show disease progression
How likely the tooth is to become mobile without treatment
How often treatment will need to be redone

cue: Miller mobility: Class 1 under 1 mm, Class 2 between 1 and 2 mm, Class 3 "goes up and down" (vertical). Just past 1 mm is already Class 2.
