stem: The Phase I case in the deck (a non-periodontitis patient with a reduced periodontium and inflamed gingiva) was diagnosed and treated how?
choices: Gingivitis on a reduced periodontium; scaling in the presence of gingival inflammation (D4346)
Stage 3 Grade B periodontitis on a reduced periodontium, treated with full-mouth scaling and root planing
Clinical health on a reduced periodontium, treated with a routine prophylaxis
Necrotizing gingivitis, treated with antibiotics and chlorhexidine rinses
ex: The patient had never had periodontitis. The bone loss was a reduced periodontium, not active disease, and the gingiva was inflamed, so the diagnosis is gingivitis on a reduced periodontium and the code is D4346.
why: Never-periodontitis patient, reduced periodontium, inflamed gingiva: gingivitis on a reduced periodontium, treated with D4346.
The patient never had periodontitis; the bone loss was a reduced periodontium, so it can't be staged and graded.
The gingiva was inflamed, so this is not clinical health and a routine prophy undertreats it.
Necrotizing gingivitis needs necrotic, painful papillae; nothing in the case points to it.

stem: Which definition matches root planing?
choices: Definitive removal of cementum or surface dentin that is rough, impregnated with calculus, or contaminated with toxins or microorganisms
Removal of supragingival stain and plaque from enamel surfaces, finished with a rubber cup and paste
Polishing the enamel and exposed root with pumice so plaque has less to hold on to afterwards
Surgical removal of the inflamed soft-tissue pocket lining (curettage), so that a new connective-tissue attachment can form against the root
ex: Scaling removes plaque, calculus and stain from supra- and subgingival surfaces (AAP Glossary, 2001).
why: Root planing is the definitive removal of rough, calculus-impregnated or contaminated cementum or surface dentin.
Removing supragingival stain and plaque with a rubber cup is coronal polishing.
Polishing enamel and root with pumice is polishing, not root planing.
Removing the inflamed pocket lining is gingival curettage, a soft-tissue procedure, not root planing.

stem: Which microbial shift is one goal of Phase I therapy?
choices: From primarily gram-negative flora toward more gram-positive flora
ex: Phase I aims to shift the subgingival flora away from gram-negative anaerobes and toward the gram-positive flora of health. Sterilizing the pocket is neither possible nor the goal.
why: Phase I aims to shift the flora from gram-negative anaerobes toward the gram-positive flora of health.
That is the reverse: disease is the shift toward gram-negative flora, and therapy undoes it.
Sterilizing the pocket is neither possible nor the goal of Phase I.
A shift toward strict anaerobes is a shift toward disease, the opposite of the goal.

stem: How does instrumentation in one session compare with multiple sessions?
choices: No considerable advantage to multiple sessions
Multiple sessions double the attachment gain
Multiple sessions remove all residual calculus
ex: Calculus left behind after multiple sessions stays for the same reasons it stays after one (Anderson et al. 1996).
why: Studies found no considerable advantage to spreading instrumentation over multiple sessions.
Multiple sessions do not double attachment gain; outcomes are similar to a single session.
Single-session therapy is not contraindicated; it works about as well as multiple sessions.
Calculus left after multiple sessions stays for the same reasons it stays after one.

cue: Hand vs ultrasonic is a tie: same PD reduction, same CAL gain.
stem: How does manual instrumentation compare with mechanically driven (ultrasonic) instrumentation?
choices: No statistical difference in PD reduction or CAL gain
Ultrasonics give significantly more CAL gain
Hand instruments give significantly more PD reduction
ex: Studies show no statistical difference between hand and ultrasonic instrumentation in PD reduction or CAL gain. Choose by access, efficiency and comfort.
why: Hand and ultrasonic instrumentation show no statistical difference in PD reduction or CAL gain.
Ultrasonics do not give significantly more CAL gain; the results are statistically similar.
Hand instruments do not give significantly more PD reduction; the results are statistically similar.
Both hand and ultrasonic instruments remove subgingival calculus.

cue: Irrigation added nothing: "the scaler does the work, the rinse just watches".
stem: What did adding subgingival irrigation (chlorhexidine, saline or peroxide) to mechanical instrumentation do?
choices: Replaced the need for root planing
ex: Adding subgingival irrigation (chlorhexidine, saline or peroxide) to mechanical instrumentation gave no additional benefit. The instrumentation does the work.
why: Adding chlorhexidine, saline or peroxide irrigation gave no additional benefit; instrumentation does the work.
Irrigation did not double PD reduction; it added nothing measurable.
Irrigation is not needed to suppress A.a.; it added no benefit beyond instrumentation.
Irrigation cannot replace root planing; it added nothing to it.

cue: Deep pockets beat the curette two times in three: about 65% of 5+ mm sites stay inadequately debrided.
stem: In pockets 5 mm or deeper, about how often is root debridement inadequate?
choices: Never, if a specialist does it
ex: Other limits on non-surgical therapy: not 100% effective against A. actinomycetemcomitans, overhanging restorations, furcations, root anatomy, hypersensitivity, operator skill, patient compliance (Greenstein 2000).
why: Root debridement is inadequate about 65% of the time in pockets 5 mm or deeper (Greenstein 2000).
5% badly underestimates it; residual calculus is the rule in deep pockets, about 65%.
25% is too low; the cited figure for pockets 5 mm or deeper is about 65%.
Even skilled operators leave calculus in deep pockets; operator skill is one of the listed limits.

stem: When is the Phase I re-evaluation done?
ex: Re-evaluate at 4–6 weeks: the connective tissue has reattached and the maximum PD reduction has happened by then.
why: At 4-6 weeks the tissue has reattached and the maximum PD reduction has already happened.
One week is too early; healing and PD reduction aren't complete yet.
Six months is far too late; nothing more is gained after 4-6 weeks and decisions get delayed.
Twelve months is far too late; re-evaluation is at 4-6 weeks.

likely.t: What SRP aims for, and re-evaluation at 4-6 weeks

cue: Most PD reduction is the swelling going down (and the recession it leaves), not new attachment.
stem: After SRP, where does most of the probing-depth reduction come from?
choices: Resolution of inflammation and edema, with the recession that follows
New bone formation at the base of the defect
New connective-tissue attachment forming on the freshly planed cementum
Tooth extrusion as the inflamed tissue shrinks back
ex: The biggest PD changes happen in the first 4 weeks.
why: Most PD reduction comes from inflammation and edema resolving (seen as recession), plus some reattachment at the base.
Non-surgical therapy does not regenerate bone at the defect base.
SRP heals mainly by a long junctional epithelium and reattachment, not new connective-tissue attachment that makes most of the change.
The tooth does not extrude after SRP; the gingiva shrinks as inflammation resolves.

stem: After SRP, how long until the dentogingival junction is re-established?
ex: Gradual repair and maturation can continue for 9-12 months (deck). In class Dr. Kaur split it up: junctional epithelium 7-10 days, connective tissue reattachment 4-6 weeks, collagen maturation 3-6 months.
why: The dentogingival junction is re-established about 2-4 weeks after SRP.
24 hours is far too short for any epithelial or connective-tissue reattachment.
9-12 months is how long repair and maturation can continue, not when the junction is re-established.
Six months is too long; the junction is back within 2-4 weeks, with collagen maturing over 3-6 months.

likely.t: What SRP aims for, and re-evaluation at 4-6 weeks

cue: A failed Phase I gets more treatment (antimicrobials, host modulation, repeat SRP, surgery), never a step down to prophy.
stem: Phase I therapy has failed at re-evaluation. Which of these is NOT one of the recommended next steps?
choices: Move the patient to routine 6-month prophylaxis
ex: First assess tissue response, remaining deposits, health history/risk factors, and possibly a plaque culture. Options are antimicrobials, host modulation, repeat non-surgical therapy, re-evaluation, or Phase II surgery.
why: This is the exception: a failed Phase I patient needs more therapy, not a downgrade to routine 6-month prophys.
Antibiotics or antimicrobials are a listed next step after Phase I fails.
Repeating non-surgical therapy is a listed option after failure.
Phase II periodontal surgery is a listed option after failure.

cue: Sickle = sharp point, triangle cross-section, above the gum. Curette = rounded toe, half-circle, below.
stem: Which feature belongs to a sickle scaler and not to a curette?
choices: Pointed tip with a triangular cross-section
ex: A sickle scaler has a pointed tip, a triangular cross-section and two cutting edges, and belongs supragingivally. A rounded toe and a half-circle cross-section are curette features.
why: A pointed tip with a triangular cross-section is the sickle scaler design.
A rounded toe is a curette feature, not a sickle feature.
A half-circle cross-section is a curette feature.
Curettes, not sickles, are safe for deep subgingival work; the sickle's point can injure tissue.

stem: Which describes a Gracey curette?
choices: 70° blade angle, one cutting edge, rounded back, lower shank parallel to the long axis of the tooth
Two cutting edges and a pointed tip, used supragingivally and subgingivally
Triangular cross-section, one cutting edge, pointed tip, used supragingivally only on anterior teeth
90° blade angle, two cutting edges, straight shank, used with a push stroke on any tooth surface
ex: Gracey curettes have the blade offset at 70°, one cutting edge (the lower one), a rounded back, and a lower shank held parallel to the tooth's long axis.
why: Gracey curettes: 70° blade offset, one cutting edge, rounded back, lower shank parallel to the tooth's long axis.
Two cutting edges and a pointed tip describe a sickle scaler.
A triangular cross-section and pointed tip describe a sickle; Graceys have a rounded back and toe.
A 90° blade with two edges describes a universal curette; Graceys are offset at 70° with one edge and a pull stroke.

cue: "Close to enter, open to clean": insert at ~0°, work at 70-80°.
stem: How is a Gracey curette inserted and then activated?
choices: Closed angle to insert into the sulcus or pocket, then a 70-80° working angle against the root
Inserted at 90° to the root and kept at that angle for the whole working stroke
Inserted open at 80° so the blade clears the tissue, then closed down to 0° against the root to do the work
Inserted at 45° and worked with a push stroke toward the base of the pocket
ex: Insert with the face closed against the root (near 0°) so the blade slips under the tissue safely, then open to a 70–80° working angle to engage and remove deposits.
why: Insert closed (near 0°) to slip under the tissue, then open to a 70-80° working angle to engage deposits.
90° is too open to insert safely and too open to work the root effectively.
That is backwards: insertion is closed and the working angle is open at 70-80°.
Curettes are inserted closed and worked with a pull stroke, not a push stroke at 45°.

stem: How far below the gingival margin can a sickle scaler remove calculus?
choices: To the base of any pocket
ex: This is the deck's number. In class Dr. Kaur said about 2-3 mm, adding that sources give 1-3 or 1-2. Sickles work mainly supragingivally with a short, powerful pull stroke, using the lower third of the blade. Use on exposed cementum is restricted.
why: The deck gives 1-2 mm below the margin (Dr. Kaur said about 2-3 mm in class).
5-6 mm is deep subgingival work, which needs curettes, not a sickle.
Sickles can't safely reach the base of a deep pocket; their use is mainly supragingival.
Sickles can remove calculus slightly below the margin, about 1-2 mm.

cue: Sickles work at about 80°, near the top of the curette's 70-80° range, with a pull stroke.
stem: What is the working angle of the H6/7 anterior sickle and the S204SD9 posterior sickle against the tooth?
ex: H6/7 has a straight shank for anteriors and the buccal/lingual of molars. S204SD9 has a right-angled shank for posterior interproximals. Both use a pull stroke.
why: Both the H6/7 and S204SD9 sickles work at about 80° to the tooth with a pull stroke.
45° is too closed to engage calculus effectively with a sickle.
110° is too open; the blade would gouge rather than engage the deposit.
0° is the closed insertion angle, not a working angle.

cue: 13/14 has the most bends because it has to reach around to the distal: the farthest reach needs the most bends.
stem: Which Gracey has more bends in its shank than the 11/12 and uses a pull stroke apico-coronally or postero-anteriorly?
ex: The Gracey 13/14 has the most bends in its shank so it can reach around to distal surfaces, and it is used with a pull stroke.
why: The 13/14 has more shank bends than the 11/12 so it reaches distal surfaces, with a pull stroke.
The 3/4 is the anterior Gracey, with a simpler shank than the 11/12.
The 15/16 is a mesial-posterior variant of the 11/12, not the most-angled distal instrument.
The Columbia 13/14 is the universal curette, not a Gracey.

cue: Scaling = short, strong chops; planing = long, light shaves.
stem: How does a root-planing stroke differ from a scaling stroke?
choices: Longer, shaving stroke with lighter pressure
ex: Scaling strokes are controlled, short, overlapping and powerful.
why: Root planing uses longer, lighter shaving strokes to smooth the root.
Short, powerful strokes describe scaling, not root planing.
The two strokes differ: scaling is short and powerful, root planing longer and lighter.
Root planing uses a pull stroke, not a push stroke.

stem: What characterizes an exploratory stroke?
choices: Light force with the instrument adapted, to map pocket depth, topography and calculus
Tight grasp and firm lateral pressure against the tooth to break calculus loose
A rubber cup held at 90° with light, intermittent pressure on the enamel surface
A pull stroke with the toe of the sickle to lift supragingival calculus off the tooth
ex: An exploratory stroke uses a light grasp and light pressure with the instrument adapted, to feel the pocket depth, root topography and calculus before any working stroke.
why: An exploratory stroke uses light force with the instrument adapted to map depth, topography and calculus.
A tight grasp with firm lateral pressure describes a working (scaling) stroke.
A rubber cup at 90° with light, intermittent pressure describes polishing.
Pulling with the sickle's toe to lift calculus is a working scaling stroke, not exploration.

stem: Match each intraoral finger rest to where it sits.
pairs: Tooth surfaces right next to the working area
The other side of the same arch
Index finger or thumb of the non-working hand
ex: Conventional rests sit right beside the working area; cross-arch on the other side of the same arch; opposite-arch on the other jaw; finger-on-finger on the non-working hand.

likely.t: Instrumentation: finger rests, scaling vs root planing, what the ultrasonic can't do

cue: Magnetostrictive = "Metal stacks, Moves in a loop, every side works". Piezo = "Pushes in a line, sides work".
stem: Match each ultrasonic type to how its tip works.
pairs: Nickel-iron metal stacks; elliptical/orbital motion, so every tip surface works
Crystals in the handpiece; linear motion, mainly the lateral surfaces work
ex: Magnetostrictive units vibrate metal stacks in an elliptical path, so every surface of the tip works. Piezoelectric crystals move the tip in a line, so mainly its lateral surfaces work.

stem: Which areas are most commonly missed during scaling and root planing?
choices: The CEJ, furcation entrances, line angles, and distal surfaces of posterior teeth
Facial surfaces of the anterior teeth, where the gingiva is thinnest and the roots most visible
Occlusal surfaces of the molars, where calculus forms fastest
Palatal surfaces of the maxillary incisors, and nowhere else in the mouth
ex: The CEJ, furcation entrances, line angles and distal surfaces of posterior teeth are the spots most often missed: hard to see, hard to reach and easy to under-instrument.
why: The CEJ, furcation entrances, line angles and posterior distals are hard to see and reach, so they're most often missed.
Anterior facials are easy to see and reach, so they are not the commonly missed areas.
Occlusal surfaces are not where SRP is done; root surfaces are.
Maxillary incisor palatals are not the classic missed sites; distals, line angles, furcations and the CEJ are.

stem: How are implant probes calibrated?
choices: They are not; implants are never probed
ex: Implant instruments in the deck: anterior and posterior sickle scalers and the Columbia 4R/4L curette.
why: Implant probes are marked in 3 mm sections, such as 3-6-9-12 or 3-6-8-11.
1 mm marks to 15 mm describe a UNC-15 periodontal probe.
Colored 5 mm bands are not the implant-probe marking described; those come in 3 mm sections.
Implants are probed routinely; that is why there are implant probes.

cue: UNC-15 = "University of North Carolina, 15 mm": a probe marked every millimeter to 15.
stem: What is a UNC-15?
choices: A periodontal probe calibrated to 15 mm
A furcation probe, curved and unmarked
An explorer for checking root roughness
An implant probe with plastic markings
ex: A UNC-15 is a periodontal probe marked at every millimeter out to 15 mm.
why: A UNC-15 is a periodontal probe marked at every millimeter out to 15 mm.
A curved, unmarked-style furcation probe describes the Nabers probe.
Checking root roughness is the job of an explorer such as the ODU 11/12.
Plastic-marked implant probes are calibrated in 3 mm sections, not the UNC-15.

cue: "4 µm in 30 s": half a minute of pumice can take the fluoride-rich top layer of enamel.
stem: How much enamel can 30 seconds of polishing with pumice paste remove?
ex: Thirty seconds of polishing with pumice can remove up to 4 µm of enamel: micrometers, so 0.004 mm, not 0.4 mm. That outermost layer holds the highest fluoride concentration, which is part of the case against routine polishing.
why: 30 seconds with pumice can remove up to 4 µm of enamel, the fluoride-rich outer layer.
40 µm is ten times the cited figure of 4 µm.
0.4 mm (400 µm) is a hundred times the cited figure.
Pumice is abrasive; it does remove enamel, up to 4 µm in 30 seconds.

cue: "2 minutes of pumice = no sulcular epithelium": keep polishing light and selective.
stem: What can a rubber cup with pumice do to the gingiva in 2 minutes?
ex: Two minutes of rubber cup and pumice can strip the sulcular epithelium completely, one reason polishing is kept selective and light.
why: Two minutes of rubber cup with pumice can strip the sulcular epithelium completely.
Polishing does not regenerate attachment; it can injure the soft tissue.
1 mm of enamel is far beyond what polishing removes (about 4 µm in 30 seconds).
Pumice polishing does not permanently seal dentinal tubules.

stem: Which polishing technique does the deck recommend?
choices: Low-abrasion paste, slow-speed handpiece, minimal heat, cup at 90° with intermittent light pressure
Coarse paste at high speed with steady, heavy pressure so stain comes off in one pass
Pumice for a full 2 minutes per tooth, with the cup held flat and pressed firmly against the surface
Subgingival polishing down to the base of the pocket with a pointed rubber cup
ex: Polish with a low-abrasion paste on a slow-speed handpiece, keep heat down, and hold the cup at 90° with light, intermittent pressure to limit enamel and tissue loss.
why: Low-abrasion paste, slow speed, minimal heat, cup at 90° with light, intermittent pressure limits enamel and tissue loss.
Coarse paste, high speed and heavy pressure remove more enamel and build heat, the opposite of what's taught.
Two minutes of pumice per tooth with heavy pressure can strip the sulcular epithelium and remove enamel.
Polishing is not done subgingivally to the pocket base; it is selective and coronal.

cue: Polish for looks and prep: stain off before sealants or fluoride. It treats nothing below the gum.
stem: Which is a valid reason FOR polishing?
choices: Removing extrinsic stain before sealants or fluoride, and patient satisfaction
Removing subgingival calculus that the curette left behind on the root
Reducing probing depth by smoothing the soft-tissue side of the pocket wall
Removing endotoxin that is bound to the cementum of the root surface
ex: Polishing removes extrinsic stain, preps teeth for sealants or fluoride, and patients like it. It does nothing for subgingival calculus, pocket depth or endotoxin.
why: Removing extrinsic stain before sealants or fluoride, and patient satisfaction, are the valid reasons for polishing.
Polishing can't remove subgingival calculus; that takes curettes or ultrasonics.
Polishing does nothing to the soft-tissue pocket wall or probing depth.
Polishing doesn't address root-bound endotoxin; root instrumentation does.

stem: The mucogingival part of the exam records which two things?
choices: The amount of keratinized gingiva and the location of the mucogingival junction
Probing depth and bleeding on probing at each of the six sites around every tooth
Mobility and fremitus, tested with two instrument handles and a finger on the teeth
Furcation class and root-trunk length on every multi-rooted tooth in the mouth
ex: The mucogingival exam records the width of keratinized gingiva and where the mucogingival junction sits.
why: The mucogingival exam records keratinized gingiva width and where the mucogingival junction sits.
PD and BOP at six sites are the probing portion of the exam, not the mucogingival part.
Mobility and fremitus are part of the occlusal/mobility exam.
Furcation class and root trunk are recorded in the furcation exam.

stem: After chewing a disclosing tablet, why does the patient rinse only briefly with water before you show them the result?
choices: Rinsing longer would stain the enamel and pellicle as well
Rinsing lightly clears loose dye while the plaque stays stained
The tablet needs a few minutes to stain the gingiva as well
A brief rinse keeps the dye from staining existing restorations
ex: The rinse is only meant to clear loose dye. Plaque holds on to the stain, so after a light rinse (and wiping excess dye off the cheeks and tongue) only the plaque stays colored, and you hand the patient a mirror to show them where it is. Disclosing shows presence of plaque, not how much.
why: Rinsing longer would wash dye off the plaque; it would not stain enamel or pellicle more.
A light rinse clears loose dye while the plaque holds the stain, so only plaque stays colored.
The tablet stains plaque on chewing; there is no waiting period to stain the gingiva.
The brief rinse is about clearing loose dye from everything but the plaque, not protecting restorations.

stem: List the occlusal findings the deck links to periodontal disease.
answer: Parafunctional habits, tooth mobility, fremitus, tooth migration, open contacts, atypical tooth wear and wear facets, possible TMJ pain, infrabony defects, and a widened PDL space.

stem: Which instrument does the deck call the most important one in the periodontal exam?
ex: The probe measures PD and CAL, outlines pocket form, and contributes to plaque, gingival and calculus assessment.
why: The deck names the periodontal probe the most important exam instrument: it gives PD, CAL and pocket form.
The ODU 11/12 explorer checks root roughness; it is not called the most important exam instrument.
The mirror gives vision, light and retraction, but can't measure the periodontium.
The Nabers probe is for furcations only.

stem: During Phase I, how do you check whether you scaled and root planed well?
choices: Explore the root surface during the session, then judge tissue response (less erythema, edema and BOP) at re-evaluation
Take a radiograph the same day and compare the calculus visible interproximally with the pre-op film to confirm that it is gone
Measure new bone fill at one week, since good root planing produces radiographic bone gain by then
Ask whether the patient reports sensitivity afterwards, since smooth, clean roots are always sensitive
ex: The patient's oral hygiene plays a fundamental role in how the re-evaluation looks.
why: Explore the root during the session, then judge tissue response (less erythema, edema and BOP) at re-evaluation.
Radiographs are poor at showing small calculus deposits and don't confirm clean roots the same day.
SRP does not produce radiographic bone fill, let alone at one week.
Sensitivity is a possible side effect, not a measure of how well you root planed.

cue: No bone loss, no periodontitis: periodontitis can only live on a reduced periodontium.
stem: Which diagnosis is impossible by definition?
ex: Bone loss is what separates periodontitis from health and gingivitis, so periodontitis always sits on a reduced periodontium. Health and gingivitis can each be on an intact or a reduced periodontium.
why: Periodontitis always involves bone loss, so it can never sit on an intact periodontium.
Gingivitis on a reduced periodontium is a real diagnosis, as in the post-ortho extraction case.
Health on a reduced periodontium is a real diagnosis, such as a stable treated patient.
Gingivitis on an intact periodontium is the ordinary gingivitis diagnosis.

stem: You run the probe about 1 mm into each sulcus and score 1 where plaque comes out and 0 where it doesn't. What does this record?
choices: Presence or absence of plaque only
The amount of plaque at each site
Plaque thickness in the gingival third
ex: Neither this method nor disclosing tablets quantifies plaque. Quantifying (gingival third, half the tooth, whole tooth) at every site would take too much chair time.
why: This method scores 1 or 0 at each site, so it records only presence or absence of plaque.
Scoring 1 or 0 doesn't quantify plaque; measuring amount at every site would take too much chair time.
Plaque thickness in the gingival third is a quantified index, which this method doesn't give.
Probing depth is measured to the pocket base, not by sweeping 1 mm into the sulcus.

stem: You finish probing the upper right and move to the upper left. Looking back, a few upper-right sites that didn't bleed at first are now bleeding. How are they scored?
choices: As not bleeding (0), because bleeding must be immediate
Re-probe them at the next visit
ex: Delayed bleeding still counts as BOP.
why: Delayed bleeding still counts as BOP, so those sites are scored 1.
Bleeding doesn't have to be immediate; delayed bleeding counts.
Waiting for the next visit is unnecessary; delayed bleeding is recorded now as BOP.
Suppuration is pus, a separate finding; these sites are bleeding.

stem: A heavy smoker has periodontitis. Compared with a non-smoker, how will the gingiva tend to look?
choices: Less inflamed, more cyanotic, because nicotine vasoconstriction masks inflammation
More edematous and hemorrhagic, because nicotine increases blood flow to the gingival tissues
Bulbous interdental overgrowth, similar to the enlargement seen with calcium channel blockers
Exactly the same, since smoking changes bone levels but has no visible effect on the gingiva
ex: Smoking masks inflammation. Diabetes does the opposite and exaggerates it.
why: Nicotine's vasoconstriction masks inflammation, so smokers' gingiva looks paler and more cyanotic.
Nicotine reduces blood flow, so tissue looks less edematous and hemorrhagic, not more.
Bulbous interdental overgrowth is drug-induced (calcium channel blockers), not a smoking look.
Smoking does change how gingiva looks: it masks the signs of inflammation.

stem: A hypertensive patient has bulbous gingival enlargement, mostly interdental and more on the buccal/labial than the lingual/palatal. Which medication fits?
ex: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker, a classic cause of drug-induced gingival overgrowth.
why: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker, a classic cause of drug-induced gingival overgrowth.
Metformin, a diabetes drug, is not associated with gingival overgrowth.
Atorvastatin, a statin, is not a cause of gingival overgrowth.
Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor; the overgrowth classic among antihypertensives is calcium channel blockers.

stem: A site probes 5 mm and the gingival margin sits 3 mm coronal to the CEJ (recession −3 mm). What is the CAL?
ex: CAL = PD + GR = 5 + (−3) = 2 mm. Skipping the recession would record CAL 5 mm and push the case toward Stage 3 or 4.
why: CAL = PD + GR = 5 + (−3) = 2 mm.
5 mm is just the probing depth; it ignores the negative recession and over-diagnoses.
8 mm adds 3 as if it were positive recession; the margin is coronal to the CEJ, so it's −3.
3 mm is just the recession value, not the attachment level.

likely.t: CAL = PD + recession, with its sign: negative recession in Salud

cue: In health the gum sits above the CEJ, so recession is negative and PD ≠ CAL.
stem: In periodontal health on an intact periodontium, how do probing depth and CAL compare?
choices: They are not equal, because the gingival margin sits coronal to the CEJ
They are always equal, since in health the CEJ and the gingival margin sit at the same level
CAL is always larger than PD, because some attachment is lost normally with age
CAL can't be measured in health, because the CEJ is covered and can't be found
ex: The margin hides the CEJ, so recession is negative and PD ≠ CAL.
why: In health the margin sits coronal to the CEJ, so recession is negative and PD does not equal CAL.
In health the gingival margin is coronal to the CEJ, not level with it, so they're not equal.
Attachment loss is not a normal part of health; CAL is smaller than PD in health.
CAL can be measured in health by feeling for the CEJ with the probe.

likely.t: CAL = PD + recession, with its sign: negative recession in Salud

stem: In Salud, what happens if you leave the recession field blank at a site with negative recession?
choices: Salud sets CAL equal to PD, over-diagnosing disease
Salud estimates the recession from the radiograph
Salud flags the site and won't save
ex: Typing 0 without checking has the same effect. Enter the signed value (+ or −) and Salud calculates CAL correctly.
why: A blank (or 0) recession makes Salud set CAL = PD, over-diagnosing disease where recession is negative.
Salud has no link to the radiograph; it uses what you enter.
Salud doesn't refuse to save; it quietly records CAL as PD.
Salud doesn't record CAL as zero; it treats recession as zero, so CAL equals PD.

likely.t: CAL = PD + recession, with its sign: negative recession in Salud

stem: How do you measure negative recession when you can't see the CEJ?
choices: Probe to the pocket base, withdraw slowly until you feel the CEJ, and read how much probe is still under the margin
Read the bone crest off a bitewing, then subtract the probing depth from that bone-level measurement
Sweep a Nabers probe horizontally along the margin and record the first point where it catches
Record recession as zero, because a CEJ you cannot see clinically means the gingival margin still sits coronal to it on that tooth
ex: That reading is the negative GR, which you subtract from PD to get CAL.
why: Probe to the base, withdraw slowly until you feel the CEJ, and read how much probe stays under the margin.
A bitewing shows the bone crest, not the CEJ-to-margin distance clinically, so it can't give recession.
A Nabers probe is a furcation instrument, not a way to find the CEJ under the margin.

pbox: PD 5 mm on #14 mesial; BOP 40%; Class II furcation on #30; 4 mm vertical (angular) defect on #19 mesial
#3, extracted 2 years ago because of periodontitis
stem: Which of these findings, on its own, places this case in Stage 3 or 4?
ex: A Class II or III furcation is one of the three automatic Stage 3/4 triggers; the other two in this box are the 4 mm vertical defect (≥3 mm) and #3 lost to periodontitis. Probing depth and bleeding don't stage a case, and a former smoker gets no grade modifier.
why: A Class II or III furcation is one of the three automatic Stage 3/4 triggers.
A 5 mm pocket on its own doesn't stage a case; CAL and complexity factors do.
Bleeding on probing reflects inflammation and plays no part in staging.
Former smoking gives no modifier, and smoking affects grade, not stage.

likely.t: Stage 4 complexity factors (the 2018 AAP/EFP tables)

cue: Grafting bone? "Full flap, two doors, mattress": full-thickness to reach bone, trapezoidal (two releases) to advance, horizontal mattress to close.
pbox: Vertical ridge augmentation (large bone graft) at the #29-30 site before implants
Thick keratinized tissue; the graft will need passive, tension-free closure
stem: Which choices fit this surgery? Select all that apply.
choices: A trapezoidal flap with two vertical releasing incisions
Horizontal mattress sutures for the layered closure
Chromic gut sutures for the graft closure
ex: Bone augmentation needs a full-thickness flap to expose bone; a split-thickness flap leaves the periosteum on the bone, so it cannot be grafted on. Major augmentation needs two releases (trapezoidal) for passive coronal advancement, with the verticals at the line angles, never mid-papilla. Horizontal mattress is the layered-closure suture for augmentation. Chromic gut is weak and resorbs in 7-10 days, too soon for a graft closure.
why: Bone augmentation needs a full-thickness flap that exposes the bone to graft on.
Major augmentation needs two vertical releases (trapezoidal) for passive, tension-free advancement.
Horizontal mattress sutures are the layered-closure suture for augmentation.
A split-thickness flap leaves periosteum on the bone, so the graft can't go on bone.
Chromic gut is weak and resorbs in 7-10 days, too soon for a graft closure.

pbox: Vertical ridge augmentation (large bone graft) at the #29-30 site before implants
Thick keratinized tissue; the graft will need passive, tension-free closure
stem: Which flap and closure fit this surgery?
choices: Full-thickness trapezoidal flap (two vertical releases at the line angles), closed in layers with horizontal mattress sutures
Split-thickness envelope flap closed with interrupted sutures
Full-thickness triangular flap with one vertical incision through the middle of the papilla
Full-thickness trapezoidal flap closed with chromic gut sutures
ex: Bone augmentation needs a full-thickness flap to expose bone, and major augmentation needs two releases (trapezoidal) for passive coronal advancement, with the verticals at the line angles, never mid-papilla (black triangle). Horizontal mattress is the layered-closure suture for augmentation. Chromic gut is weak and resorbs in 7-10 days, too soon for a graft closure.
why: Full-thickness trapezoidal flap with releases at the line angles, closed in layers with horizontal mattress sutures.
A split-thickness flap leaves periosteum on the bone, and an envelope flap can't advance passively over a large graft.
A vertical through the middle of the papilla risks a black triangle; one release isn't enough for major augmentation.
The flap is right, but chromic gut resorbs in 7-10 days, too soon to hold a graft closure.

pbox: Generalized Stage 3 Grade C periodontitis, treated with SRP and osseous surgery last year
stem: What maintenance interval fits this patient?
choices: No maintenance is needed once pockets are ≤4 mm
ex: Once periodontitis, always higher risk, and he's a current heavy smoker. Pathogens repopulate in about 9-11 weeks, which is why high-risk patients are seen about every 3 months.
why: A treated Stage 3 Grade C patient who still smokes heavily is high risk; pathogens repopulate in 9-11 weeks.
Six months is for low-risk patients; pathogens return in about 9-11 weeks, well before 6 months.
A 12-month interval would leave a high-risk patient unsupervised far too long.
Once periodontitis, always at risk; treated patients need lifelong maintenance.

likely.t: Risk-stratified maintenance intervals

pbox: Little plaque or inflammation; 8-11 mm pockets on #14 and the first molars
Deep, narrow vertical bone defects on those teeth
stem: Which diagnosis fits the case Dr. Geisinger reviewed in class?
choices: Localized Stage 3 Grade C periodontitis, molar-incisor pattern
ex: Stage 3: vertical bone loss of 3 mm or more is an automatic Stage 3 trigger, and the 8-11 mm pockets sit over deep vertical defects. Localized, molar-incisor pattern: only the first molars and #14 are involved. Grade C: that much bone loss at 13 gives a bone-loss/age ratio well over 1.0. Not gingivitis (there is bone loss), not generalized, and Grade A would mean slow progression, the opposite of this case. The plan was regeneration, closer lifelong maintenance and counseling against nicotine.
why: Vertical defects trigger Stage 3, molar-incisor pattern makes it localized, and this much loss at 13 is Grade C.
Only the first molars and #14 are involved, so it's localized, and loss this fast at 13 is Grade C, not B.
Deep pockets over vertical bone defects mean periodontitis, not gingivitis.
Grade A means slow progression; heavy bone loss at age 13 is rapid, Grade C.

pbox: Bulbous gingival enlargement, mostly interdental, worse on the buccal/labial
PD 5 mm; gingival margin sits 3 mm coronal to the CEJ
stem: What is the clinical attachment level at #8 mesial?
ex: Recession is −3 mm, so CAL = 5 + (−3) = 2 mm. Leaving recession blank (or 0) in Salud would record CAL 5 and over-diagnose disease.
why: Recession is −3 mm, so CAL = 5 + (−3) = 2 mm.
5 mm is the probing depth; using it as CAL ignores the negative recession and over-diagnoses.
8 mm treats the recession as +3; the margin is coronal to the CEJ, so it's −3.
0 mm would need the probe to stop at the CEJ; the pocket extends 2 mm past it.

likely.t: CAL = PD + recession, with its sign: negative recession in Salud

pbox: Heavy generalized calculus covering the gingival margins and parts of the occlusal surfaces; the margin can't be seen or explored
stem: What is the appropriate first appointment?
choices: Full-mouth debridement, then a comprehensive periodontal evaluation in about 2 weeks
Full-mouth debridement and SRP of all four quadrants the same day
Periodontal charting from the calculus surface, then SRP
ex: Debridement is only for when you can't see or explore the margin, it's never combined with SRP, and insurance won't pay for it plus an exam the same day. (At school, first charting is free, so faculty may let you chart the same visit.)
why: Margins can't be seen or explored, so debride first, then do the comprehensive evaluation in about 2 weeks.
Debridement is never combined with SRP, and SRP can't be planned before a diagnosis.
A prophylaxis is preventive care for a diagnosed, healthy-to-gingivitis mouth; this mouth can't yet be diagnosed.
Charting from the calculus surface gives meaningless numbers; the margin has to be visible first.

pbox: Second premolars extracted for orthodontics as a teen; never diagnosed with periodontitis
Generalized red, swollen gingiva; BOP 60%; lingual bridge of calculus
Mild bone-level loss next to the premolar extraction sites and molar tipping; no other bone loss
stem: Which procedure fits this patient?
choices: Scaling in the presence of generalized moderate or severe gingival inflammation (D4346)
ex: Gingival inflammation on a reduced periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient. It sits between a prophy and SRP, is done with perio faculty, and gets a Phase I evaluation.
why: Gingival inflammation on a reduced periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient is D4346.
She's never had periodontitis; bone loss from extraction sites doesn't make it periodontitis, so SRP doesn't fit.
Maintenance is only for patients already treated for periodontitis.
Debridement is only when margins can't be seen or charted; nothing says that here.

pbox: SRP of all quadrants 5 weeks ago for Stage 3 Grade B periodontitis
Most sites improved; #3 and #14 still bleed and probe 6 mm; the probe catches residual calculus on both roots
stem: What is the best next step?
choices: Remove the residual calculus and re-evaluate in 2 weeks
Wait 3 more months for additional pocket reduction
ex: Residual deposits explain the persistent disease, so remove them and re-evaluate in two weeks. Waiting past 4-6 weeks adds no pocket reduction, and more SRP where the roots are already clean won't help (improve oral hygiene instead).
why: Residual calculus explains the persistent sites, so remove it and re-evaluate in two weeks.
Surgery is considered only after the cause (residual calculus) is removed and the sites re-evaluated.
Most sites responded; only two sites need attention, not a full-mouth repeat.
Maximum PD reduction is reached by 4-6 weeks; waiting longer adds nothing.

pbox: Tissue looks pale and fibrotic, with less redness than expected for 6-7 mm pockets
stem: Which statements about this patient are consistent with the Session 4 lecture? Select all that apply.
choices: Nicotine's vasoconstriction can mask inflammation, giving a paler, cyanotic look
His outcome after even excellent SRP may be poorer short- and long-term
Uncontrolled diabetes tends to exaggerate the inflammatory picture
His pale tissue means BOP can be skipped
SRP will reverse his bone loss if he quits smoking
ex: Smoking masks, diabetes exaggerates. The host response shapes healing, so 'failure of therapy' is more likely. BOP is always recorded, and non-surgical therapy never reverses bone loss.
why: Nicotine vasoconstriction masks inflammation, giving a paler, cyanotic look, as in this patient.
The host response shapes healing, so smokers and uncontrolled diabetics do worse even after excellent SRP.
Uncontrolled diabetes exaggerates inflammation, the opposite effect of smoking.
BOP is always recorded; pale tissue doesn't mean it can be skipped.
Non-surgical therapy never reverses bone loss, even if he quits smoking.

pbox: Tissue looks pale and fibrotic, with less redness than expected for 6-7 mm pockets
stem: What best explains how his tissue looks?
choices: Nicotine's vasoconstriction masks the inflammation, giving a paler, cyanotic look
Uncontrolled diabetes hides inflammation, so the tissue looks pale
The pale tissue means the disease is inactive, so BOP can be skipped
Fibrotic tissue means his bone loss will reverse after SRP if he quits smoking
ex: Smoking masks, diabetes exaggerates, so the pale look is the cigarettes, not quiet disease. BOP is always recorded, non-surgical therapy never reverses bone loss, and his host response makes a poorer outcome after even excellent SRP more likely.
why: Nicotine constricts the gingival vessels, so smokers' tissue looks paler and more fibrotic than their pockets would predict: smoking masks inflammation.
Diabetes does the opposite: uncontrolled, it exaggerates the inflammatory response, so it wouldn't make the tissue look pale.
Pale tissue in a smoker hides disease rather than proving it's inactive, and BOP is always recorded anyway.
Non-surgical therapy never reverses bone loss, and quitting smoking improves healing but doesn't regrow bone.

stem: Which modifiers can move a periodontitis case to Grade C regardless of the bone-loss/age ratio? Select all that apply.
choices: Smoking 10 or more cigarettes a day
ex: Modifiers only push the grade up. Not smoking or not having diabetes never earns a downgrade.
why: Belongs: smoking 10 or more cigarettes a day is a grade modifier that pushes the case to Grade C.
Belongs: HbA1c of 7% or higher in a diabetic patient is a modifier that pushes the case to Grade C.
Doesn't belong: modifiers only push the grade up; not smoking never moves a case to Grade C (or down).
Doesn't belong: HbA1c under 7% is below the Grade C cutoff, so well-controlled diabetes doesn't force Grade C.
Doesn't belong: age is used in the bone-loss/age ratio itself, not as a separate modifier.

likely.t: Grading: start at B; the bone-loss/age ratio, smoking and HbA1c

cue: Gingivitis = "swollen, bleeding, reversible, nothing lost": pseudopockets to 4-5 mm, BOP, no CAL and no bone loss.
stem: Which are true of plaque-induced gingivitis? Select all that apply.
choices: There is no attachment loss or bone loss
It is reversible with plaque control
Bone loss is limited to the coronal third
ex: 4-5 mm depths are possible because swollen gingiva makes pseudopockets with no attachment loss. Bone loss, even limited to the coronal third, makes it periodontitis, so that choice is false. The course uses a 10% full-mouth BOP threshold before calling a case gingivitis.
why: Belongs: swollen gingiva can create pseudopockets of 4-5 mm with no attachment loss.
Belongs: bleeding on probing is the hallmark of plaque-induced gingivitis (the course uses a 10% full-mouth BOP threshold).
Belongs: gingivitis is confined to the gingiva, with no attachment or bone loss.
Belongs: gingivitis resolves once the plaque is controlled; that reversibility separates it from periodontitis.
Doesn't belong: any bone loss, even in the coronal third, makes the case periodontitis, not gingivitis.

cue: Phase I removes causes: hygiene, SRP, smoking advice, caries control, bad margins. "Never forget: caries control is Phase I."
stem: Which belong in Phase I (non-surgical) therapy? Select all that apply.
ex: Phase I removes the causes: oral hygiene instruction, SRP, smoking-cessation counseling, caries control and fixing plaque-retentive margins. 'Never forget this: caries control is part of Phase I.' Osseous surgery is Phase II (surgical), and final crowns wait until periodontal therapy is complete.
why: Belongs: oral hygiene instruction is the core of Phase I, which removes the causes of disease.
Belongs: caries control is part of Phase I; the lecture stressed never forgetting it.
Belongs: fixing plaque-retentive margins removes a local cause of plaque, so it's Phase I.
Doesn't belong: osseous (resective) surgery is Phase II, the surgical phase.
Doesn't belong: final crowns are Phase III (restorative) and wait until periodontal therapy is done.

stem: Which recession types predict at least partial root coverage? Select all that apply.
ex: RT1 (no interproximal loss) predicts full coverage and RT2 (interproximal loss no greater than the buccal) partial. RT3 isn't attempted.
why: Belongs: RT1 has no interproximal attachment loss, so full root coverage is predicted.
Belongs: in RT2 the interproximal attachment loss is no greater than the buccal, so partial coverage is predicted.
Doesn't belong: in RT3 the interproximal attachment loss is greater than the buccal, so root coverage isn't attempted.

cue: "Gut and the Glycolics go away": chromic gut, PGA and PGCL resorb. Silk, PTFE and polypropylene must come out.
stem: Which suture materials are resorbable? Select all that apply.
ex: Chromic gut (7-10 days), PGA (55-70 days) and PGCL (22-55 days) resorb. Silk, PTFE and polypropylene have to be removed.
why: Belongs: chromic gut is resorbable, lasting about 7-10 days.
Belongs: poly-glycolic acid (PGA) is resorbable, lasting about 55-70 days.
Belongs: poly(glycolide-co-caprolactone) (PGCL) is resorbable, lasting about 22-55 days.
Doesn't belong: silk is non-resorbable (and braided, so it wicks plaque); it must be removed.
Doesn't belong: PTFE is a non-resorbable monofilament that has to be removed.
Doesn't belong: polypropylene is a non-resorbable monofilament that has to be removed.

likely.t: The suture chart: resorption, braided vs monofilament, tissue reaction

stem: Which follow the surgical principles taught for incisions and flaps? Select all that apply.
choices: Make the incision with a firm, continuous stroke
Place vertical incisions at the line angle
Keep the incision away from the bony defect
Make the flap base at least as wide as its free edge
Place the vertical incision in the middle of the papilla
Place the incision directly over the defect
ex: A mid-papilla vertical risks recession and a black triangle, and a narrow base starves the flap.
why: Belongs: a firm, continuous stroke gives a clean incision edge that heals well.
Belongs: vertical incisions go at the line angle, which protects the papilla and keeps the flap blood supply.
Belongs: incision lines should rest on sound bone, away from the defect, so the closed flap is supported.
Belongs: a base at least as wide as the free edge keeps the flap's blood supply.
Doesn't belong: a vertical in the middle of the papilla risks recession and a black triangle.
Doesn't belong: an incision over the defect leaves the wound margin unsupported and prone to breakdown.

likely.t: Vertical incisions at the line angle, never through the papilla

cue: "Bone needs a full flap": implants, augmentation and osseous surgery all touch bone. Soft-tissue grafts go split-thickness.
stem: Which procedures call for a full-thickness flap? Select all that apply.
ex: Soft-tissue grafting uses a split-thickness flap so the periosteum stays behind as a vascular bed for the graft.
why: Belongs: implant placement needs a full-thickness flap to expose the bone.
Belongs: bone, ridge or sinus augmentation needs the bone exposed, so the flap is full thickness.
Belongs: crown lengthening and osseous surgery reshape bone, so the periosteum is lifted with the flap.
Doesn't belong: soft-tissue grafting uses a split-thickness flap, leaving periosteum as a vascular bed for the graft.

likely.t: Full vs partial thickness by procedure

cue: UniFe = "Smoke, Sugar, Pockets, Bleeding, Bone": cigarettes/day, HbA1c, pockets ≥5 mm, BOP %, bone-loss/age. It scores bleeding, never plaque.
stem: Which inputs does the UniFe risk tool score? Select all that apply.
ex: UniFe scores five inputs, each 0-4, summed into a five-tier risk score: cigarettes a day, HbA1c, number of pockets ≥5 mm, BOP % and the bone-loss/age ratio. Plaque index and the number of furcations are not UniFe inputs. Plaque index is the favorite wrong tick: plaque starts the disease, but UniFe scores bleeding (BOP %), not plaque.
why: Belongs: cigarettes a day is one of UniFe's five inputs.
Belongs: HbA1c (diabetic status) is one of UniFe's five inputs.
Belongs: the bone-loss/age ratio is one of UniFe's five inputs.
Doesn't belong: UniFe scores bleeding (BOP %), not plaque; plaque index is the favorite wrong tick.
Doesn't belong: furcations aren't scored; UniFe counts pockets of 5 mm or more instead.

cue: Kwok & Caton asks one question: "Can we Keep it Calm?" Stability, therapeutic only, questionable in the middle, works for complex patients.
stem: Which statements describe the Kwok & Caton prognosis system? Select all that apply.
choices: It asks whether periodontal stability can be achieved
Questionable sits in the middle of its scale
It works well for medically complex patients
It is scored numerically from smoking and A1c
ex: Molars-only and numeric scoring describe Miller & McEntire.
why: Belongs: Kwok & Caton bases prognosis on whether periodontal stability can be achieved.
Belongs: the system is therapeutic only, judging the outcome of treatment.
Belongs: questionable sits in the middle of its scale, between favorable and unfavorable.
Belongs: because it centers on stability rather than a fixed formula, it works well for medically complex patients.
Doesn't belong: molars-only describes Miller & McEntire, not Kwok & Caton.
Doesn't belong: numeric scoring from factors like smoking describes Miller & McEntire, not Kwok & Caton.

likely.t: Kwok & Caton (stability, whole dentition) and Miller & McEntire (molars)

stem: Which are the P's of P4 medicine? Select all that apply.
ex: Personalized, preventive, predictive and participatory (some add a fifth P). It's set against one-size-fits-all Hippocratic medicine.
why: Belongs: personalized is one of the four P's.
Belongs: preventive is one of the four P's.
Belongs: predictive is one of the four P's.
Belongs: participatory is one of the four P's: the patient takes part in their care.
Doesn't belong: palliative care isn't one of the P's of P4 medicine.
Doesn't belong: prescriptive sounds like a P but isn't one; P4 is set against one-size-fits-all medicine.

cue: Anything that covers the CEJ (swelling, overgrowth, altered passive eruption) or mimics it (calculus, a margin) hides it from the probe.
stem: Which make it harder to feel the CEJ when measuring negative recession? Select all that apply.
choices: Healthy tissue with a visible CEJ
ex: Inflammation and overgrowth are pathologic, altered passive eruption is physiologic, and calculus or margins can feel like a CEJ.
why: Belongs: heavily inflamed, swollen tissue covers the CEJ and makes it hard to feel (pathologic).
Belongs: drug-induced overgrowth covers the CEJ with excess tissue (pathologic).
Belongs: altered passive eruption leaves gingiva over the CEJ (physiologic).
Belongs: calculus or a restorative margin can feel like the CEJ and mislead the probe.
Doesn't belong: in true recession the margin is apical to the CEJ, so the CEJ is exposed, not hidden.
Doesn't belong: a visible CEJ in healthy tissue is easy to find.

cue: SRP goals are "calm, shift, stop": reduce inflammation, shift the flora to gram-positive, arrest progression. It doesn't rebuild or eliminate pockets.
stem: Which are goals of scaling and root planing? Select all that apply.
choices: Shift the flora from gram-negative toward gram-positive
ex: The goals are to reduce inflammation, shift the flora from gram-negative toward gram-positive and arrest disease progression: all three belong. SRP doesn't reverse lost bone or attachment, and pocket elimination isn't its rationale, though PD does drop.
why: Belongs: SRP removes plaque and calculus, which reduces inflammation.
Belongs: SRP shifts the flora from gram-negative anaerobes toward a gram-positive, health-associated flora.
Belongs: SRP aims to arrest disease progression.
Doesn't belong: SRP doesn't reverse bone or attachment loss; it stops it from progressing.
Doesn't belong: pocket elimination isn't SRP's rationale, though probing depth does drop.

cue: Pocket shrinks from both ends: the top drops (edema resolves into recession) and the bottom seals (JE, then connective tissue). No new bone.
stem: Which contribute to probing-depth reduction after SRP? Select all that apply.
ex: At the margin, resolving edema shows up as more recession. At the base, JE (7-10 days) and connective tissue (4-6 weeks) reattach to the clean root. SRP doesn't regrow bone.
why: Belongs: as edema resolves the margin moves apically, so more recession accounts for part of the PD drop.
Belongs: junctional epithelium reattaches to the clean root in about 7-10 days, at the pocket base.
Belongs: connective tissue reattaches to the root in about 4-6 weeks, adding to the PD reduction.
Doesn't belong: SRP doesn't regrow bone; new bone fill takes regenerative therapy.
Doesn't belong: the tooth doesn't extrude after SRP; PD drops from recession and reattachment.

cue: Debridement is a "clear the view" visit: full mouth only, not therapy, only when you can't see the margin, never with SRP.
stem: Which statements about full-mouth debridement are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: It is not a therapeutic procedure
It is indicated only when you can't see or explore the gingival margin
There is only a full-mouth code
It should never be combined with SRP
It can be billed per quadrant
Insurance pays for it and a periodontal exam at the same visit
ex: There is no quadrant or half-mouth code, and insurance won't pay for debridement plus an exam the same day, so the exam is usually about 2 weeks later.
why: Belongs: debridement isn't therapeutic; it clears heavy deposits so a proper exam can be done.
Belongs: it's indicated when deposits keep you from seeing or exploring the gingival margin.
Belongs: there is only a full-mouth code, no quadrant or half-mouth code.
Belongs: it should never be combined with SRP; definitive therapy follows the exam.
Doesn't belong: there is no quadrant code for debridement; it's billed full mouth only.
Doesn't belong: insurance won't pay for debridement and an exam the same day, so the exam is usually about 2 weeks later.

cue: SRP is a root-surface job: anything that lives off the root (bacteria in the soft-tissue wall) or blocks the blade (grooves, furcations, margins, blind access) is a limitation.
stem: Which are limitations of scaling and root planing discussed in class? Select all that apply.
choices: It is a blinded, tactile procedure
Motile bacteria invade the pocket lining
It can't be done with local anesthesia
ex: All but the last are on the list. The one most often left unticked is motile bacteria: they invade the soft-tissue pocket lining, and SRP only reaches the root surface in the pocket. Local anesthesia is not a limitation: SRP is routinely done with it. Also on the list: pocket depth and access, patient compliance with hygiene, and operator skill.
why: Belongs: SRP is done blind and by feel under the gingiva, which limits it.
Belongs: motile bacteria invade the soft-tissue pocket lining, which SRP can't reach (the most often missed tick).
Belongs: overhanging or subgingival margins hold plaque and block instrumentation.
Belongs: grooves, concavities and furcations are hard to reach with instruments.
Belongs: over-removing cementum exposes dentin and causes hypersensitivity.
Doesn't belong: SRP is routinely done under local anesthesia, so anesthesia isn't a limitation.

stem: Which can a radiograph tell you before you probe? Select all that apply.
choices: Whether bone loss is localized or generalized
ex: BOP is a clinical finding. Dr. Kaur's tip: keep the x-rays open during SRP, not the chart.
why: Belongs: a radiograph shows whether bone loss is localized or generalized.
Belongs: a radiograph shows whether bone loss is horizontal or vertical.
Belongs: root proximity and fused roots are visible on a radiograph.
Belongs: calculus is often radiopaque and visible on a radiograph.
Belongs: a periapical lesion shows on the radiograph.
Doesn't belong: bleeding on probing is a clinical finding that only probing can show.

cue: "Buccal is a bottleneck": the maxillary buccal furcation entrance is the narrowest, because the two buccal roots sit close together.
stem: On maxillary molars, which furcation entrance is the narrowest?
ex: On maxillary molars the straight buccal entrance, between the mesiobuccal and distobuccal roots, is generally narrower than the mesiopalatal and distopalatal entrances, whose roots splay farther apart. Narrowest is not closest: the mesiopalatal entrance is the one nearest the CEJ (about 3.6 mm, vs buccal about 4.2 mm).
why: The buccal entrance, between the mesiobuccal and distobuccal roots, is generally the narrowest on maxillary molars.
The mesial (mesiopalatal) entrance is the closest to the CEJ, not the narrowest; its roots splay farther apart.
The distal (distopalatal) entrance is the deepest from the CEJ, and its roots diverge more than the buccal's.
The entrances differ in width; the buccal is generally the narrowest.

stem: On maxillary molars, how far from the CEJ is the distal furcation entrance?
ex: As taught (Bower 1979), the maxillary first molar's entrances sit about 3.6 mm (mesiopalatal), 4.2 mm (buccal) and 4.8 mm (distopalatal) from the CEJ; the exam-review guide rounds them to 3, 3.5 and 5 mm. Either way the distal one is the most apical. About 8 mm is the maxillary premolar's.
why: The distal (distopalatal) entrance is the most apical: about 5 mm in the exam-review guide (4.8 mm as taught).
About 3 mm is the guide's figure for the mesial entrance, the one closest to the CEJ.
About 3.5 mm is the guide's figure for the buccal entrance.
About 8 mm is the maxillary premolar's furcation depth, not the molar's.

likely.t: Bower's furcation entrance depths from the CEJ

stem: Which molar has a shorter root trunk — the first or the second maxillary molar?
ex: The first molar has the shorter root trunk, so its furcation starts closer to the CEJ and is exposed by less attachment loss.
why: The first molar has the shorter root trunk, so less attachment loss reaches its furcation.
The second molar's trunk is longer, so its furcation sits farther from the CEJ.
The trunks differ; the first molar's is shorter.
Both molars have a measurable root trunk between the CEJ and the furcation.

stem: On mandibular molars, which furcation entrance is both wider and more apical — buccal or lingual?
ex: On mandibular molars the lingual entrance is wider (a slide gives over 0.75 mm) and more apical than the buccal, because the molar is angled lingually. In the lecture's numbers (Bower) the difference is small: buccal about 2.4 mm, lingual about 2.5 mm from the CEJ.
why: The lingual entrance is wider and slightly more apical, because mandibular molars are angled lingually.
The buccal entrance is the narrower and slightly more coronal one (about 2.4 mm vs 2.5 mm from the CEJ).
They differ slightly: the lingual is wider and more apical.
It doesn't vary randomly; the lingual angulation of the molar makes the lingual entrance more apical.

likely.t: Bower's furcation entrance depths from the CEJ

stem: Roughly what percentage of maxillary premolars have two root cones?
ex: About 40% of maxillary premolars have two root cones, which is why they can have a furcation (mean ≈8 mm from the CEJ).
why: About 40% of maxillary premolars have two root cones, so they can have a furcation.
About 10% is too low; about 40% of maxillary premolars have two roots.
About 75% is too high; about 40% of maxillary premolars have two roots.
About 5% is too low; about 40% of maxillary premolars have two roots.

cue: Class I = "just the doorway": smooth the entrance (furcation plasty) and root plane. No surgery for a catch.
stem: Furcation Class I is best managed with which treatment?
ex: A Class I furcation is only incipient, so SRP plus furcation plasty (smoothing the entrance so it can be cleaned) is enough.
why: A Class I furcation is incipient, so SRP plus furcation plasty (smoothing the entrance) is enough.
Extraction is far too aggressive for an incipient Class I furcation; it's an option for advanced Class II-III.
Root resection is limited to deep Class II and Class III furcations.
GTR (regeneration) is a Class II option, not needed for an incipient Class I.

stem: The exam-review guide lists GTR as a Class II furcation option for which teeth?
ex: The guide lists GTR for Class II mandibular molars. The lecture adds the buccal furcation of maxillary molars as an equally good candidate; their mesial and distal (interproximal) degree II furcations are much less suited because access is limited.

stem: Which bone architecture pattern has interdental bone sitting apical to its midfacial and midlingual margins?

stem: Why does osseous surgery reshape the bone to follow the gingiva?

stem: When is the Phase I re-evaluation done?

stem: Which is NOT a purpose of Phase I therapy on Dr. Litz's slides?

Insurance requires at least two cleanings before any surgery

stem: According to the 1981 study on root planing, what happens in pockets deeper than 5 mm?

Calculus removal is as complete as in shallow pockets

stem: Which is NOT one of the three reasons residual calculus increases with pocket depth?

There is more root surface to scale

stem: In positive osseous architecture, the interproximal crest is:

Apical to the midfacial and midlingual bone
At the same level as the midfacial bone
Below the root apex on a radiograph

stem: On a radiograph of healthy periodontium, about how far is the interproximal crest from the adjacent CEJs?

Facial bone has no attachment to the root

stem: Which statement best separates a furcation from a furcation defect?

stem: The root trunk is the part of the root between:

The furcation fornix and the root apex
The CEJ and the root apex
The alveolar crest and the furcation fornix

stem: On average, about how much of a molar's periodontal attachment is on its root trunk?

About 50% is too high; roughly 30% is on the trunk and 70% on the roots.

cue: Long trunk = good goalie, bad rescue: it keeps the furcation closed longer, but once it opens, the short roots left can't be saved by resection.
stem: Why is a long root trunk only initially a favorable feature?
choices: Once the furcation is reached, little root is left in bone and the tooth is a poor candidate for resection

stem: What is an intermediate bifurcation ridge?

stem: Restoration margins placed apical to the free gingival margin should:

stem: What does a tunnel preparation deliberately create?

stem: Which root is removed most often in root resection?
