Regeneration offers degree III furcations no advantage over conventional surgery.
Long root trunks make teeth poor resection candidates, not ideal ones.
Mandibular molar furcations are probed with a Nabers probe routinely.

cue: Contributing factors you can FIX: CEP, enamel pearl, overhang, the ridge (odontoplasty). Root trunk length you can't.
stem: Which local factors that contribute to furcation involvement can the clinician remove or alter? Select all that apply.
ex: CEPs and small enamel pearls can be removed with a bur (odontoplasty), and overhangs corrected. Root trunk length and the molar's angulation are anatomy you can't change, though they affect risk and treatment choice.
why: Belongs: a CEP can be removed with a bur (odontoplasty).
Belongs: an overhang can be corrected or replaced.
Belongs: a small enamel pearl can be removed with a bur.
Doesn't belong: root trunk length is fixed anatomy, though it affects risk and treatment.
Doesn't belong: the molar's lingual angulation is anatomy you can't change.

stem: Which make a patient a poor candidate for furcation regeneration, as taught? Select all that apply.
choices: A root canal filling in the tooth
ex: Uncontrolled diabetes, immunocompromise, smoking, poor compliance and poor hygiene all count against regeneration. A root canal filling is not a contraindication, and a thicker biotype favors success.
why: Belongs: uncontrolled diabetes counts against regeneration.
Belongs: smoking counts against regeneration.
Belongs: poor hygiene and compliance doom regeneration; the patient must keep it clean.
Doesn't belong: a root canal filling is not a contraindication.
Doesn't belong: a thicker biotype favors success.

stem: Which statements about root resection are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: It commits the patient to endodontic and restorative treatment
It is limited to deep Class II and Class III furcations
The distobuccal root of the maxillary first molar is removed most often
It removes the root together with its part of the crown
It is the first choice for teeth with long root trunks
ex: Removing the root with its part of the crown is hemisection. Long root trunks generally make teeth poor candidates for resection.
why: Belongs: resection requires endodontics first and restoration after.
Belongs: resection is limited to deep Class II and Class III furcations.
Belongs: the maxillary first molar's distobuccal root is removed most often.
Doesn't belong: removing the root with its part of the crown is hemisection; resection leaves the crown.
Doesn't belong: long root trunks mean short roots, which make teeth poor resection candidates.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Maxillary molars are affected by furcation involvement more often than mandibular molars.
2. On maxillary molars, the distopalatal furcation is affected most often.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false: the buccal furcation is affected most, then the mesiopalatal, then the distopalatal.
why: Statement 2 is false: on maxillary molars the buccal furcation is affected most, not the distopalatal.
Statement 1 is true: maxillary molars are affected more often than mandibular molars.
Statement 1 is true, and statement 2 is false: the buccal is most affected, then mesiopalatal, then distopalatal.
Statement 1 is true, and statement 2 is false: the distopalatal is affected least, not most.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. New attachment will not form on enamel.
2. Every cervical enamel projection should be removed when it is found.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Statement 1 is true, which is why CEPs are a problem. Statement 2 is false: with no bone or attachment loss (often Grades 1 and 2), usually no treatment is needed; remove it once loss is associated with it.
why: Statement 2 is false: a CEP without bone or attachment loss usually needs no treatment.
Statement 1 is true: no connective-tissue attachment forms on enamel, which is why CEPs cause trouble.
Statement 1 is true (no attachment to enamel), and statement 2 is false: remove a CEP only once loss is associated with it.
Statement 1 is true, not false, and statement 2 is false: not every CEP needs removal.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The Glickman and Hamp classifications describe horizontal furcation destruction.
2. Tarnow and Fletcher subclass C means 7 mm or more of vertical destruction.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Both are true. Tarnow and Fletcher add the vertical component in 3 mm steps: A 0-3 mm, B 4-6 mm, C 7 mm or more.
why: Both are true: Glickman and Hamp grade horizontal loss, and Tarnow and Fletcher subclass C is 7 mm or more vertical.
Both statements are true, not false.
Statement 2 is also true: subclass C is 7 mm or more (A 0-3, B 4-6).
Statement 1 is also true: Glickman and Hamp both describe horizontal destruction.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A furcation arrow on a radiograph should not be the sole tool for detecting furcation involvement.
2. Furcation arrows are typically seen at the buccal furcation of mandibular molars.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Statement 1 is true: many involved furcations show no arrow. Statement 2 is false: arrows mark mesiopalatal and distopalatal lesions of maxillary molars. Mandibular molar furcation bone loss is usually easy to see directly.
why: Statement 2 is false: arrows mark mesiopalatal and distopalatal furcations of maxillary molars.
Statement 1 is true: many involved furcations show no arrow, so it can't be the sole tool.
Statement 1 is true, and statement 2 is false: mandibular molar furcation bone loss is usually seen directly, without an arrow.
Statement 1 is true, not false, and statement 2 is false: arrows are a maxillary molar sign.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Tunneling is limited to mandibular molars with sufficiently long, divergent roots.
2. Hemisection converts a multi-rooted tooth into a single-rooted tooth.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Both are true. Tunneling creates a Glickman Grade IV so a brush can pass through; hemisection removes a root with its part of the crown, usually on mandibular molars.
why: Both are true: tunneling needs long, divergent mandibular molar roots, and hemisection makes a single-rooted tooth.
Both statements are true, not false.
Statement 2 is also true: hemisection removes a root with its part of the crown, leaving one root.
Statement 1 is also true: tunneling is limited to mandibular molars with long, divergent roots.

stem: All of the following are contributing factors for furcation involvement EXCEPT:
choices: A long interradicular dimension (widely spaced roots)
ex: Widely spaced roots are favorable: instruments reach in, in SRP and in surgery. Closely approximated or fused roots are the contributing factor. CEPs, overhangs and intermediate bifurcation ridges all hold plaque.
why: This is the exception: widely spaced roots are favorable, letting instruments reach in; close or fused roots contribute.
CEPs are a contributing factor: no connective-tissue attachment forms on enamel, so plaque is funneled into the furcation.
Overhangs are a contributing factor: they hold plaque near the furcation.
Intermediate bifurcation ridges are a contributing factor: they leave a plaque trap above them.

stem: All of the following are recommended for a Class II furcation EXCEPT:
ex: Class II recommendations: furcation plasty, regeneration (GTR), root resection or extraction. Observation without therapy fits early (Class I) involvement with no alterable local factor.
why: This is the exception: observation without therapy fits early Class I involvement with no alterable local factor.
Furcation plasty is a recommended Class II option.
Regeneration (GTR) is a recommended Class II option.
Root resection is a recommended option for deep Class II furcations.

stem: All of the following are true of cervical enamel projections EXCEPT:
choices: They occur more often on maxillary than mandibular molars
They are more likely on second molars
They are more likely on the buccal surface
ex: The reverse: about 30% of mandibular molars vs about 15% of maxillary molars. The rest are true.
why: This is the false one: CEPs are more common on mandibular molars (about 30%) than maxillary (about 15%).
True: CEPs are more likely on second molars.
True: CEPs are more likely on the buccal surface.
True: a Grade 3 CEP extends into the furcation.

stem: All of the following are steps of furcation regeneration surgery as taught EXCEPT:
choices: Leaving enamel projections in place to support the graft
A sulcular incision with a full-thickness flap
Securing a barrier membrane with a resorbable sling suture
ex: Root anomalies such as enamel projections and pearls are removed, since no connective-tissue attachment forms on enamel. The flap is then secured coronally, and the patient skips mechanical plaque removal at the site for up to 4 weeks.
why: This is the exception: enamel projections and pearls are removed, since no connective-tissue attachment forms on enamel.
A step: access is through a sulcular incision with a full-thickness flap.
A step: the exposed root surfaces are cleaned before grafting.
A step: the barrier membrane is held with a resorbable sling suture.

stem: In the root resection sequence, all of the following should be avoided EXCEPT:
choices: Removing alveolar bone defects around the remaining roots
Leaving parts of the furcation fornix behind
Leaving sharp angles on the remaining roots
ex: Periodontal surgery to remove bone defects around the remaining roots is part of the sequence. When separating the roots, avoid exposing the interradicular bone, leaving fornix behind, perforating the canals and leaving sharp angles.
why: This is the exception: removing bone defects around the remaining roots is part of the sequence, not avoided.
Avoided: exposing the interradicular bone when separating the roots.
Avoided: leaving parts of the fornix behind, which leaves a plaque trap.
Avoided: sharp angles on the remaining roots, which can't be cleaned and concentrate stress.

stem: Match each furcation classification to what it measures.
pairs: Grades I-IV by how far the probe goes, up to visible through-and-through
Degrees 1-3 by millimeters of horizontal loss
Subclasses A-C by millimeters of vertical loss
ex: Glickman (1953) and Hamp (1975) both describe horizontal destruction (Hamp in millimeters: under 3, over 3, through). Tarnow and Fletcher (1984) add the vertical component: A 0-3, B 4-6, C 7+ mm.

stem: What depth and angle make an intrabony defect the best candidate for regeneration?
choices: Any depth — angle does not matter
ex: The best regenerative candidates are deep, narrow intrabony defects: more than 3 mm deep and 25° or less to the root. Deep, narrow walls hold the clot and the cells that rebuild the tissue.
why: Deep (over 3 mm) and narrow (under 25°) defects hold the clot and cells best, so they regenerate most predictably.
Shallow, wide defects are the poorest candidates: they can't hold the clot.
Depth and angle both matter; deep, narrow defects do best.
There's no 10 mm requirement; over 3 mm deep with a narrow angle is the target.

likely.t: Best candidates: deep, narrow, 3-wall defects

stem: Which wall configuration is the best candidate for periodontal regeneration?
ex: A 3-wall defect has the most bony walls to hold the clot and supply cells, so it regenerates most predictably. 1-wall defects are the least predictable.
why: A 3-wall defect has the most bony walls to hold the clot and supply cells, so it regenerates most predictably.
1-wall defects are the least predictable for regeneration.
A 2-wall crater has fewer walls than a 3-wall defect, so it's less predictable.
A defect with no walls can't contain a clot or graft, so it's the poorest candidate.

likely.t: Best candidates: deep, narrow, 3-wall defects

stem: What are amelogenins, the active component of EMD, involved in?
choices: Enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during tooth development
Only pulp formation, guiding odontoblasts as they lay down dentin inside the developing tooth
Only cementum resorption, clearing the root surface so that the PDL fibers can re-insert
Bacterial biofilm formation, which is why EMD is always paired with a systemic antibiotic
ex: Amelogenins, the main enamel matrix proteins, drive enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during tooth development. EMD borrows that to regrow attachment.
why: Amelogenins drive enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during development; EMD borrows that.
Amelogenins are enamel matrix proteins; they don't direct odontoblasts or pulp formation.
They support new attachment formation, not cementum resorption.
Amelogenins have nothing to do with biofilm, and EMD isn't required to be paired with a systemic antibiotic.

likely.t: Biologics: EMD (amelogenins), rhPDGF-BB, β-TCP

stem: What does rhPDGF-BB do in a regenerative graft?
choices: Chemotactic/mitogenic for bone and PDL, and angiogenic for revascularization
Purely antibacterial, for infection control only
ex: rhPDGF-BB draws in bone and PDL cells (chemotactic), makes them multiply (mitogenic) and grows new vessels (angiogenic).
why: rhPDGF-BB is chemotactic and mitogenic for bone and PDL cells, and angiogenic for new blood vessels.
PDGF is a growth factor, not an antibacterial agent.
PDGF is a growth factor, not a steroid.
Collagenase inhibition is how subantimicrobial-dose doxycycline works, not PDGF.

likely.t: Biologics: EMD (amelogenins), rhPDGF-BB, β-TCP

stem: What is the primary role of a β-TCP scaffold in a regenerative graft?
choices: Osteoconductive matrix that prevents soft-tissue collapse and stabilizes the clot
Antibiotic delivery, releasing drug slowly into the defect to suppress pocket bacteria after surgery
Replacing the need for a flap, because the scaffold can be injected through the pocket without surgery
Bleaching and conditioning the root surface so that cementum can reform on the treated root
ex: β-TCP is the scaffold: an osteoconductive matrix that keeps soft tissue from collapsing into the defect and holds the clot still.
why: β-TCP is an osteoconductive scaffold: it keeps soft tissue from collapsing into the defect and holds the clot still while bone grows in.
β-TCP carries no antibiotic. Slow local drug release is what products like Arestin or Atridox do, not a graft scaffold.
A regenerative graft still needs a flap for access and debridement; β-TCP is packed into an opened defect, not injected through the pocket.
β-TCP does not condition the root. Root conditioning uses separate agents (such as EDTA); the scaffold's job is space and clot stability.

likely.t: Biologics: EMD (amelogenins), rhPDGF-BB, β-TCP

stem: Which of these is a risk factor for a less predictable regenerative outcome?
ex: A thin, scalloped gingival biotype is a risk factor for a less predictable regenerative result. The other three choices describe a good defect for regeneration.
why: A thin, scalloped biotype is more likely to recede and expose the graft, so it makes a regenerative result less predictable.
A 3-wall defect is the most favorable for regeneration: the walls contain the graft and supply blood and cells.
A narrow defect angle (under 25°) is a favorable feature, since a narrow defect holds the clot and graft well.
A deeper defect (over 3 mm) is a favorable feature for regeneration, not a risk factor.

likely.t: Risk factors for a less predictable result

stem: EMD, alone or combined with graft material, produces outcomes similar to which other regenerative approach?
ex: EMD, used alone or with graft material, produces outcomes similar to GTR.
why: EMD, alone or with graft material, gives outcomes similar to GTR, the other main regenerative approach.
Gingivectomy is a resective procedure that removes tissue; it regenerates nothing.
Root planing alone heals by repair with a long junctional epithelium, not regeneration of lost attachment.
Systemic antibiotics are an adjunct to mechanical therapy, not a regenerative technique.

likely.t: Biologics: EMD (amelogenins), rhPDGF-BB, β-TCP

stem: List the three biologic modifications discussed for periodontal regeneration and one property of each.
answer: EMD — an amelogenin extract that supports attachment formation; rhPDGF-BB — a chemotactic, mitogenic, and angiogenic growth factor; β-TCP scaffold — an osteoconductive matrix that stabilizes the clot.

stem: As defined at the 1996 World Workshop, periodontal regeneration is the formation of which tissues?
choices: New bone, new cementum and new PDL
New bone and a long junctional epithelium
New cementum and new gingival epithelium
New bone and new keratinized gingiva
ex: Regeneration means new bone, new cementum and new PDL: a new functional attachment apparatus over a root that disease had exposed. Bone fill alone, or epithelium against the root, is not regeneration.
why: All three, forming a new functional attachment apparatus over a pathologically exposed root.
A long junctional epithelium against the root is repair, not regeneration.
Epithelium on the root is what regeneration tries to prevent; bone and PDL are missing too.
Keratinized gingiva is soft tissue above the attachment; cementum and PDL are missing.

likely.t: Regeneration vs repair; only histology proves it

stem: What separates regeneration from repair?
choices: Regeneration restores the original architecture and function
Regeneration happens only when a membrane is placed
Repair needs a graft, while regeneration needs none
Repair forms new cementum, while regeneration doesn't
ex: Repair closes the wound without restoring the original architecture and function; regeneration rebuilds the attachment apparatus. After a flap or root planing, a root usually heals by repair: a long junctional epithelium.
why: Regeneration rebuilds bone, cementum and PDL as they were; repair heals without restoring them.
Grafts and biologics can regenerate without a membrane; GTR is one route, not the definition.
Neither term is defined by the material used; repair is how a root heals with no graft at all.
It's the reverse: new cementum is part of regeneration, while repair usually leaves epithelium on the root.

likely.t: Regeneration vs repair; only histology proves it

stem: After open flap debridement, a long junctional epithelium lines the treated root. What is this healing called?
ex: Epithelium growing down the root is the usual result of flap or root-planing healing: repair. It can be stable, but it isn't a new attachment apparatus.
why: Healing without new cementum and inserting PDL fibers is repair.
Regeneration needs new cementum, PDL and bone, not epithelium against the root.
Osseointegration is bone bonding to an implant surface, not healing on a root.
Guided bone regeneration grows bone for implants on a ridge; it says nothing about the root's attachment.

likely.t: Regeneration vs repair; only histology proves it

stem: Besides cells, scaffolds and growth factors, which factor in periodontal tissue regeneration does the deck list?
ex: The slide's four factors: cells, scaffolds, growth factors and blood supply.
why: Blood supply keeps the clot and the new tissue alive: the fourth factor on the slide.
Antibiotics are adjuncts for infection; they aren't one of the four factors.
Occlusal adjustment may help a mobile tooth, but it isn't one of the four factors.
Extrusion changes the bone level orthodontically; it isn't one of the four factors.

stem: Which radiographic findings were reported as most amenable to conventional GTR?
choices: Depth over 3 mm and an angle of 25° or less
Depth under 3 mm and an angle of 25° or less
Depth over 3 mm and an angle of 45° or more
Depth under 3 mm and an angle of 45° or more
ex: Defects deeper than 3 mm with a radiographic defect angle of 25° or less were most amenable to conventional GTR-based regeneration.
why: Deep and narrow: the combination on the slide.
Narrow is right, but shallow defects gain less.
Deep is right, but a wide angle can't contain the clot or graft.
Shallow and wide is the worst combination for regeneration.

stem: According to the 2021 systematic review on the slides, which intrabony defects gained the most CAL and bone 12 months after regenerative surgery?
choices: Deeper, narrower defects with more walls
Shallower, wider defects with more walls
Deeper, wider defects with fewer walls
Shallower, narrower defects with fewer walls
ex: Nibali 2021: deeper defects with narrower angles and more walls showed more CAL gain and radiographic bone gain at 12 months.
why: Depth, a narrow angle and more walls all improved CAL and radiographic bone gain.
Shallow, wide defects gain less, even with more walls.
A wide angle and fewer walls leave nothing to contain the clot.
Shallow defects with fewer walls gain the least.

likely.t: Best candidates: deep, narrow, 3-wall defects

stem: On the slides, what does "non-supportive" defect anatomy mean?
ex: Non-supportive anatomy is a predominantly 1-wall defect, a risk factor for failure (odds ratio of 10.4 or more).
why: Non-supportive anatomy is defined as predominantly 1-wall: a risk factor for failure.
A 3-wall defect is the most supportive, the best candidate.
A circumferential defect surrounds the root with bone, so it is well contained.
A crater is a 2-wall defect between teeth, more supportive than a 1-wall defect.

stem: In the 2012 study of minimally invasive surgery with a bovine xenograft, which pair predicted more midfacial recession?
choices: A 1-wall defect and a thin, scalloped biotype
A 3-wall defect and a thick, flat biotype
A deep defect and a narrow defect angle
Heavy smoking and a long root trunk
ex: Non-supportive anatomy (1-wall vs 2-wall) and a thin, scalloped gingival biotype were the risk factors for more midfacial recession.
why: Both were risk factors for more recession at the midfacial (Cosyn 2012).
These are the favorable findings, not the risks.
Depth and a narrow angle favor regeneration.
Neither was the finding on the slide; root trunks were a Session 5 furcation topic.

stem: Why does a 3-wall intrabony defect regenerate more predictably than a 1-wall defect?
choices: Its walls hold the clot and supply cells and vessels
Its walls stop epithelium from growing down the root
It never needs a graft, a membrane or a biologic
Its depth and width can be read exactly on a film
ex: More walls contain the defect: the clot and graft stay put, cells and vessels come from more surfaces, and the flap is held up.
why: Contained defects keep the clot and graft still and bring in cells and blood from more surfaces.
Bone walls don't block the epithelium; that is the membrane's job in GTR.
3-wall defects are still treated with grafts, membranes or biologics.
A film is 2-D; walls are confirmed at surgery, not read exactly on the radiograph.

likely.t: Best candidates: deep, narrow, 3-wall defects

stem: How is the number of remaining walls in an intrabony defect confirmed?
choices: By looking at the debrided defect at surgery
By measuring the defect angle on a periapical
By probing at six sites around the tooth
By counting the walls on a vertical bitewing
ex: A radiograph is a flat picture of a 3-D defect. The deck's opening case shows the defect from the buccal, the lingual and after debridement: that is where the walls are counted.
why: Once the flap is raised and the defect debrided, the walls can be seen directly.
The angle on a film helps select cases, but a 2-D film can't count walls reliably.
Probing finds the defect but can't show which walls remain.
Bitewings are 2-D too: walls overlap and hide each other.

stem: In Laurell's 1998 meta-analysis of open flap debridement, about how much CAL was gained?
ex: Laurell 1998 (305 defects): probing depth 7.0 to 4.0 mm, CAL gain 1.5 mm, bone gain 1.1 mm. This is the baseline regeneration has to beat.
why: 1.5 mm of CAL gain, with 1.1 mm of bone gain, over 305 defects.
4 mm was the residual probing depth, not the gain.
0.2 mm is far too little; every study on the slide gained over 1 mm.
7 mm was the initial probing depth.

stem: After open flap debridement, pockets fell from 7.0 to 4.0 mm but CAL improved only 1.5 mm. What accounts for the rest?
choices: Bone fill raising the pocket base
New cementum on the coronal root
ex: Probing depth falls by the CAL gain plus the recession. Half of the 3 mm reduction is the margin moving apically.
why: PD reduction = CAL gain + recession: 3.0 = 1.5 + 1.5.
Bone fill doesn't change the pocket depth beyond the CAL gain; it was only 1.1 mm.
New cementum would show up as CAL gain, which was only 1.5 mm.
These are averages across 305 defects, not a measuring error.

stem: What role does open flap debridement play in the regeneration studies on the slides?
choices: The baseline that regeneration must beat
A negative control with no flap reflected
A regenerative procedure using a membrane
The test group treated with a bone graft
ex: Open flap debridement (flap, debridement, no graft) gains about 1.5 mm of CAL. Grafts, GTR and biologics are measured against it.
why: Regenerative techniques are judged by what they add to open flap debridement alone.
A flap is reflected; that's what open flap debridement means.
Debridement alone has no membrane; adding one makes it GTR.
Debridement alone has no graft; it's the comparison for graft groups.

stem: In the deck's bone-graft case, what does DFDBA stand for?
ex: DFDBA is demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft: human donor bone. The deck's defect was filled with it and healed to a 3 mm probing depth.
why: DFDBA: demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft, from a human donor.
Bovine bone is a xenograft, and an autograft comes from the patient.
An alloplast is synthetic; DFDBA is human bone.
DFDBA isn't the patient's own bone, so it isn't an autograft.

stem: Where does a DFDBA graft come from?
choices: The patient's own jaw or hip
A cow, processed to remove protein
ex: Grafts are named by source: autograft (the patient), allograft (another human, e.g., DFDBA), xenograft (another species, e.g., bovine) and alloplast (synthetic, e.g., β-TCP).
why: An allograft comes from another human.
That would be an autograft.
Bovine bone is a xenograft.
Synthetic grafts such as β-TCP are alloplasts.

likely.t: Graft types and the GTR membrane

stem: What does the barrier membrane do in guided tissue regeneration?
choices: Keeps epithelium and gingival CT off the root
Releases growth factors into the bone defect
Removes the need to debride the root surface
Seals the flap edges so no sutures are needed
ex: Gingival epithelium and connective tissue grow much faster than PDL and bone. The membrane keeps them off the root so the slower cells can fill the defect.
why: Excluding the fast-growing soft tissue lets PDL and bone cells repopulate the root.
Release of growth factors is what rhPDGF-BB and EMD do; the membrane is a barrier.
The root is still debrided before the membrane goes on.
The flap is still sutured over the membrane.

likely.t: Graft types and the GTR membrane

stem: In combination therapy, what does a bone graft add under a GTR membrane?
choices: It holds the space so the membrane can't collapse
It replaces the membrane as the epithelial barrier
It releases amelogenins that coat the root
It lets the membrane be removed sooner
ex: A graft under the membrane keeps it from sagging into the defect, so there is space for the new tissue. The deck shows GTR with a bone graft.
why: The graft supports the membrane and keeps the defect space open.
The membrane is still the barrier; the graft sits under it.
Amelogenins come from EMD, not from a bone graft.
The graft doesn't change how long the membrane stays.

likely.t: Graft types and the GTR membrane

stem: What did the deck's 20- and 25-year radiographs of regenerated sites show?
choices: The regenerated bone was still there
The graft had resorbed and the defect reopened
The teeth had been lost within 10 years
The defects had become furcation lesions
ex: Radiographs at baseline, 1 year and 20 or 25 years after regeneration: the regenerated bone held up over decades.
why: The bone gained after regeneration was stable decades later.
That's the opposite of what the long-term films showed.
The teeth were still there at 20 and 25 years.
Nothing on the slides shows a conversion to furcation involvement.

stem: Why is a non-contained intrabony defect harder to treat with a biologic such as EMD alone?
choices: Nothing holds up the flap or the clot
EMD binds only to bone walls, not root
Amelogenins are inactivated in wide defects
A flap can't be raised over the defect
ex: A non-contained (1-wall or wide) defect has no walls to support the soft tissue or hold the clot, so a biologic alone has no space to work in. A graft is usually added.
why: Without walls the space collapses, so these defects usually get a graft as well.
EMD is applied to the root surface; walls aren't what it binds.
Amelogenins aren't inactivated by defect width; the problem is space.
A flap can be raised over any defect; the issue is what holds it up.

stem: Which method is the only one that can prove true periodontal regeneration?
ex: Regeneration is evaluated by histology, clinical measurements and radiographs, but only histology proves it.
why: Only a tissue section shows new cementum with inserting PDL fibers and new bone.
A probe can't tell new attachment from a long junctional epithelium.
Radiographs show bone fill, not attachment.
Subtraction shows bone change between two films, still not attachment.

likely.t: Regeneration vs repair; only histology proves it

stem: Why can't CAL gain alone prove that regeneration happened?
choices: A probe can't tell new attachment from long JE
CAL is measured from the moving gingival margin
CAL only improves when a membrane is used
Teeth aren't probed after regenerative surgery
ex: CAL gain shows the probe stops more coronally, but a long junctional epithelium (repair) resists the probe too. Only histology can tell them apart.
why: The probe stops at a long junctional epithelium just as it would at new attachment.
CAL is measured from the CEJ, a fixed point; probing depth is from the margin.
Open flap debridement alone gains about 1.5 mm of CAL with no membrane.
Sites are probed after surgery; that's how CAL gain is measured.

likely.t: Regeneration vs repair; only histology proves it

stem: What does digital subtraction radiography show?
choices: Only the change between two standardized films
The number of walls remaining in the defect
New cementum and PDL fibers on the root
ex: Subtracting two standardized radiographs leaves only the bone gained or lost. Chaves, Geurs, Reddy and Jeffcoat used it in 1996 to evaluate a bioresorbable membrane.
why: Two matched films taken at different times are subtracted, so only what changed shows.
Walls are confirmed at surgery, not on a subtraction image.
Cementum and PDL fibers need histology.
It is still 2-D: two periapicals, not a CBCT.

stem: What is MIST, on the deck's list of regenerative procedures?
choices: A membrane made of synthetic polymer
A mineralized bone graft from a donor
A medication that conditions the root
ex: MIST is the minimally invasive surgical technique: a small flap that preserves the papilla over an isolated intrabony defect.
why: MIST works through a small flap that keeps the papilla.
Membranes are GTR; MIST is a surgical technique.
Donor bone grafts are allografts such as DFDBA.
Root biomodification on the deck means EMD or PDGF, not MIST.

stem: Which two agents does the deck list under biomodification?
ex: The deck's list: bone grafts, GTR, combination therapy, biomodification (enamel matrix protein, PDGF) and MIST.
why: Biomodification on the slide: enamel matrix protein and PDGF.
These are grafts: an allograft and an alloplast.

stem: Why does Dr. Litz say to step lightly with host modulation?
choices: Too much suppression could make an infection lethal
It breeds bacterial resistance within a few weeks
Dentists aren't allowed to prescribe host modulators
It stops the gingiva from healing after scaling
ex: Down-regulate a patient's host response too far and a seemingly innocent bacterial infection could turn serious, even lethal. That caution is part of why host modulation isn't further along, even though the cellular picture has been known for years.
why: "You better know what you're doing before you start monkeying around with this."

stem: Why is bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ) so hard to treat?
choices: Scraping off the dead bone is trauma, which is what causes it
It is a bacterial infection resistant to most antibiotics
Stopping the bisphosphonate for a week reverses it, but few patients will
The exposed bone grows back too fast to debride
ex: In BRONJ the gingiva dies back and exposes bone that becomes necrotic. Dead bone left exposed will get infected, so an oral surgeon scrapes it, and that trauma is what causes BRONJ. Bisphosphonates stay in the system for years. This is why none is approved as host modulation therapy.
why: The lesion can come back bigger, the size of a quarter instead of a dime: a vicious cycle.
It isn't an infection, though it can look like one (exposed dead bone can become infected).
The drugs have a very long half-life and stay in the system for years; a short break does nothing.
Necrotic bone is dead and can't come back.

stem:
Which statements about how periodontal tissue is destroyed are true?
1. Bacteria alone are sufficient to cause attachment loss.
2. IL-1 stimulates collagenase and PGE2.
3. Complement acts mainly as a chemoattractant for PMNs.
4. Neutrophils are the first responders to a bacterial insult.
ex: Bacteria are required but not sufficient: the host response mediates the destruction. Complement calls in PMNs, neutrophils arrive first, and cytokines such as IL-1 drive collagenase, PGE2, MMPs and osteoclasts.
why: It includes 1, which is false: bacteria are required but not sufficient; the host response to them mediates the destruction. It leaves out 4, which is true: neutrophils arrive within about 24-48 hours; macrophages come later.

stem: You slide a probe into the facial sulcus of #8 and can see its outline through the gingiva. What does that tell you?
choices: A thin phenotype, 1 mm or less
A thin phenotype, 2 mm or less
ex: Phenotype thickness is judged with the probe in the sulcus: visible through the tissue = thin (1 mm or less); not visible = thick (more than 1 mm). It matters because a thin phenotype is predisposed to recession.
why: The validated test: a probe visible through the tissue means a thin phenotype, 1 mm or less of soft tissue.
It's the reverse: a thick phenotype hides the probe. Seeing it means the tissue is thin.
The cutoff is 1 mm: thin is 1 mm or less, thick is more than 1 mm.
Recession is the margin apical to the CEJ, measured from the margin to the CEJ; a probe showing through measures thickness.

stem: A young patient about to start orthodontics has no recession, but the tissue over his incisors is so thin the roots show through. Why did Dr. Abou-Arraj graft him first?
choices: To thicken a thin phenotype before tooth movement
To cover recession already present on the incisors
To deepen a shallow vestibule for the brackets
To widen the band of attached gingiva to 5 mm
ex: His thin phenotype put him at risk of recession once the teeth moved and brushing went on for years. A trapezoidal full-thickness flap, a connective tissue graft over the two central incisors and the flap back over the graft changed it to a thick phenotype, and he was cleared for orthodontics.
why: Orthodontics, then years of brushing, would put thin tissue at risk of recession; a CTG under the flap thickened it first.
He had no recession yet; the graft was to prevent it, not to cover a root.
The vestibule wasn't the problem in this case; the tissue's thickness was.
No width target was set; the goal was changing the phenotype from thin to thick.

likely.t: Thin vs thick phenotype: the probe test and recession risk

stem: How is gingival recession measured?
choices: From the gingival margin to the CEJ
From the CEJ to the base of the pocket
From the gingival margin to the pocket base
From the gingival margin to the MGJ
ex: Recession = the marginal tissue apical to the CEJ (AAP Glossary 2001). Probe from the gingival margin to the CEJ at six sites and record it so it can be followed. Note interproximal recession too: it changes the prognosis.
why: Recession is the margin's position apical to the CEJ, so it is measured margin to CEJ, at the same six sites as probing depth.
That is the clinical attachment level, which adds the recession to the probing depth.

The gingiva thins with age itself, whatever the risk factors
Older patients brush harder than younger ones

choices: A dehiscence, a thin phenotype and aggressive brushing
A fenestration, a thick phenotype and a soft brush
Gingivitis, a thick phenotype and a wide band of attached gingiva
A low frenum, a thick phenotype and flossing
ex: An anatomic variation (fenestration or dehiscence) plus a thin phenotype plus aggressive brushing is "like the perfect storm" for recession on one or more teeth.

stem: A mandibular incisor sits buccal to the arch, with thin facial tissue and recession. What can moving it back onto the arch orthodontically do?
choices: Resolve some of the recession, without a graft
Nothing: only a graft changes a recession
Cover the exposed root completely in every case
ex: A buccally positioned tooth has thinner facial tissue and takes more of the toothbrush. Repositioned onto the arch, within its alveolar housing, the tissue thickens and recession can at least partly resolve without grafting.

stem: After Phase I and resective Phase II surgery, a patient has recession on many teeth. Where did most of it come from?
choices: The surgery, which removes pockets on purpose
The periodontitis itself, before any treatment began
A thin phenotype unmasked by the surgery
ex: Previous periodontal surgery is a predisposing factor: resective therapy reduces pockets by removing tissue, which exposes root surfaces. It's done deliberately, for an environment the patient can maintain without pockets and inflammation.

Brushing trauma causes recession too, but here the resection itself exposed the roots.

stem: What did Dr. Abou-Arraj call the key word in how recession develops?
ex: Two pathways: brushing trauma (abrasion, inflammation, an ulcer, recession) and plaque (the periodontitis process on a thin phenotype). Both run through inflammation; everything on the factor list is predisposing.
why: "The key word here is inflammation": it's what actually causes recession; the factors on the list predispose to it.
Trauma starts one pathway, but it leads to recession through inflammation and ulceration.
A thin phenotype is a predisposing factor, not the cause.
Plaque starts the other pathway, but again through inflammation.

stem: A canine has 4 mm of facial recession, and the interproximal CEJ can't be found on either side. With a graft, how much root coverage can you expect?
ex: An undetectable interproximal CEJ means no interproximal attachment loss: Cairo RT1, where about 100% root coverage is possible. RT2 gives partial coverage (about 50-60% in his cases); RT3 gives none.
why: No interproximal attachment loss is RT1: the best prognosis, and full root coverage is achievable.
That is what he quoted for RT2, where interproximal attachment has been lost.
That is RT3, where interproximal loss exceeds the buccal loss.
No type in the Cairo system predicts a quarter; RT1 predicts full coverage.

stem: A tooth's interproximal CAL is 6 mm and its buccal CAL is 4 mm. Which Cairo recession type is it?
choices: It can't be typed without a radiograph
ex: Cairo: RT1 no interproximal attachment loss; RT2 interproximal CAL less than or equal to buccal CAL; RT3 interproximal CAL greater than buccal CAL. 6 mm against 4 mm is RT3.
why: Interproximal attachment loss greater than the buccal loss is RT3: root coverage won't be achieved.
RT2 has interproximal loss less than or equal to the buccal loss; here it is greater.
RT1 has no interproximal attachment loss at all; here it is 6 mm.
The Cairo types are read from the clinical attachment levels; no radiograph is needed.

stem: Why can't a graft cover an RT2 recession all the way to the CEJ?

The CEJ can't be found clinically in RT2
A coronally advanced flap can't be moved that far
RT2 roots are too sensitive for grafting
ex: In RT2 the best you can hope for is coverage up to the level of the interproximal attachment, because without bone and attachment between the teeth there is no framework or blood supply to support the tissue higher. ("If we know how to fix this, we could ... cure everybody from periodontitis.")

choices: It stays stable if it causes no symptoms
It reverses once the patient brushes gently
ex: Chambrone and Tatakis (systematic review, 2016): untreated recession continues to progress, leading to esthetic disharmony, hypersensitivity and root caries. So "let's just monitor it" doesn't keep it the same; apart from RT3, consider treatment when indicated.

stem: Why is the palate the usual donor site for gingival grafts?
choices: Its tissue is keratinized and passes that on
It has no major vessels or nerves to work around
Its wound always heals by primary intention
Its tissue is thin and elastic, like mucosa
ex: "We go to the palate because it has orthokeratinized soft tissue": the graft carries the information of keratinization to the recipient site. Palatal connective tissue induces epithelial differentiation and keratinization.
why: The palate is orthokeratinized, and its connective tissue induces keratinization at the recipient site.
The greater palatine artery and nerve run through it; harvesting means staying away from them.
An FGG donor site is left open and heals by secondary intention.
Palatal tissue is thick, firm and keratinized, unlike the alveolar mucosa.

stem: Which layer of the palate is usually the thickest, and is what a connective tissue graft is made of?
ex: From the surface in: epithelium (0.3-0.6 mm), lamina propria (connective tissue, 1.25-3.0 mm), submucosa (fat and glands), bone. An FGG is epithelium plus lamina propria; a CTG is the lamina propria alone.
why: The connective tissue layer, 1.25-3.0 mm on the slide; a CTG is this layer without the epithelium.
The surface layer is thin, 0.3-0.6 mm; an FGG includes it, a CTG doesn't.
The adipose and glandular layer under the lamina propria; it is usually trimmed off the graft.
The periosteum covers the bone under the submucosa; it isn't harvested as the graft.

likely.t: The palate: its layers, the greater palatine bundle, the high vault

stem: The graft will be covered completely by a coronally advanced flap. Which graft do you use?
choices: A CTG, since epithelium under a flap won't heal
An FGG, since its epithelium protects the root
An FGG, since it carries more keratinization
Either one, since the flap's underside is epithelium
ex: The rule: a graft that will be covered by a flap must be connective tissue only (a CTG); a graft left exposed is an FGG, with its epithelium.
why: The flap's inner side is connective tissue; epithelium placed against it "just would not heal properly."
An FGG's epithelium is for a graft left exposed; under a flap it would not heal.
Both grafts carry the palate's keratinization; the deciding question is covered or exposed.
The flap's inner side is connective tissue, which is why a covered graft must be connective tissue only.

likely.t: Which graft: a covered graft is a CTG, under a coronally advanced flap

stem: In his root-coverage case on #10 and #11, how was the flap closed over the connective tissue graft?
choices: Advanced coronally, tension free, over the graft
Positioned apically, the graft left exposed
Put back at its old level, half the graft exposed
Not closed: left to heal by secondary intention
ex: Trapezoidal partial-thickness flap, a CTG harvested and de-epithelialized, sutured over the roots, then the flap advanced coronally, tension free, covering the recessions and the graft. "We always do a coronally advanced flap if we're trying to cover the graft."
why: A coronally advanced flap covering the graft completely, tension free so it holds its coronal position.
That is the FGG approach for gaining keratinized gingiva, not root coverage with a CTG.
A CTG is covered completely; an exposed CTG would heal poorly.
The palatal donor site of an FGG heals that way; the recipient flap here was sutured over the graft.

stem: What is an acellular dermal matrix allograft?
choices: Human dermis with its epidermis and cells removed
Bovine collagen pressed into a membrane
The patient's own palatal tissue, de-epithelialized
A synthetic polymer scaffold seeded with fibroblasts
ex: ADM (AlloDerm is one) is dermis donated to a tissue bank, usually from cadavers, processed to remove the epidermis, hair follicles and cells, leaving collagen, elastic and reticular fibers. It is the most common soft tissue allograft.
why: Processed skin from a tissue bank: a matrix of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers, with no cells.
Bovine and porcine products exist, but ADM is human dermis.
That is a connective tissue graft, an autograft.
ADM is processed human tissue with the cells removed, not a seeded synthetic.

stem: Which case best suits an acellular dermal matrix instead of a palatal graft?
choices: Root coverage on six teeth in one surgery
A band of KG on one tooth, the graft left exposed
Thickening the tissue on one central incisor
A demanding site where every cell helps healing
ex: ADM's advantages: no donor site, more patient acceptance, shorter surgery, many defects in one procedure, results comparable to autogenous tissue, ease of use. Its limits: it must be covered, and in demanding sites it can't match the patient's own tissue.
why: No donor site and "unlimited" quantity: multiple defects in one procedure, as in his canine-to-canine case.
ADM must be covered; creating KG with an exposed graft is an FGG's job.
One tooth needs only a small palatal harvest; he used a CTG for exactly this.
ADM has no cells to contribute; in a demanding site autogenous tissue does better.

stem: Why must an acellular dermal matrix be covered completely by the flap?
choices: It has no cells or blood supply to heal on its own
Left exposed, the body rejects it as foreign tissue
Its epidermis can't heal against the flap
Saliva dissolves the matrix within days
ex: ADM has nothing to contribute to healing, so it is fully covered, usually with a coronally advanced flap. Over time it is remodeled and replaced by the patient's own tissue, as histology has shown.
why: "More or less a dead piece of skin," like a band-aid; covered, it is remodeled and replaced by the patient's tissue.
His reason was the lack of cells and blood supply, not rejection.
ADM has no epidermis; it is removed in processing.
His reason was that it can't heal by itself without a blood supply.

likely.t: The acellular dermal matrix: what it is, when, and why it's covered

stem: What sets a tunnel (pouch) flap apart?

It has two vertical releasing incisions
It is positioned apically to expose the graft
It is raised full thickness all the way down to the bone crest

stem: How is the width of keratinized gingiva measured?
choices: From the gingival margin to the MGJ
From the CEJ to the MGJ
From the gingival margin to the sulcus base

stem: In Meffert's terms, this implant is
ex: Meffert: ailing, static bone loss without inflammation or mobility (monitor); failing, progressive bone loss with inflammation but no mobility (treat, or keep in function); failed, progressive loss with mobility and loss of function (remove). stem: Why does her history of periodontitis matter for this implant?
choices: It doesn't, once the teeth are out

ex: Why the patient lost their teeth matters: susceptibility to periodontitis raises the risk of peri-implant disease. Her periodontitis was treated before the implant, which was right; missing three years of maintenance was not. Compliance with plaque control and maintenance decides the result.
why: A patient who lost teeth to periodontitis is a susceptible host; periodontitis and peri-implantitis share bacteria, and putative pathogens can persist a year after the teeth come out.

why: Interproximal CAL 3 mm is less than the 4 mm buccal CAL: RT2, coverage up to about the interproximal attachment level.

RT3 needs interproximal loss greater than the buccal; here 3 mm is less than 4 mm.
cue: Compare interproximal CAL with buccal CAL: none = RT1, less or equal = RT2, more = RT3.
